Console

The read-mostly observability UI at /console - the complete list of what it can change, how sign-in works, the three experience levels, and what each page shows.

The console is the owner's window onto a system whose actual clients are agents. It is html/template plus vanilla JS plus SSE, served by internal/console from the same binary as everything else - no node, no npm, no React, no build step. It is not how Seamless is driven; it is how you watch it.

The console's own words use no double hyphen and no em or en dash. A title an agent wrote (a plan's, a task's, a note's, a trial's) shows its " -- " as a colon wherever the console draws it. That is display only: the stored title, what a copy button copies, the JSON answers and every body keep what the agent wrote, so a command such as git checkout -- path in a body stays intact.

What the console can change

The console is read-mostly. That is a design claim, so here is the whole list - every write it is capable of, taken from the POST routes in internal/console/console.go. There are no others. A few of those routes write nothing, and their rows say so.

Action Route Effect
Archive a memory POST /console/memories/{id}/archive Routes through lifecycle.Archive: the memory is stamped invalid and leaves briefings, recall and every index. Its file stays on disk with a line saying when it was archived, its history stays readable here, and Restore a memory brings it back. Records memory.archived with by: console. Returns to the Memories list or the memory's own page next= names, its filters kept; any other next returns to the plain list. An archived memory is left as it is.
Restore a memory POST /console/memories/{id}/restore Routes through lifecycle.Restore, under the file's lock: an archived memory, or a superseded one that nothing active replaced, comes back into briefings, recall and the indexes, and the line its retirement added to the body comes off. Refused (409), with nothing written, while a memory that replaced it is still active (the answer names that memory when you can read it), and while Held holds it: with write screening on, its file is quarantined or the review flagged it, and, whenever the held queue is served, an agent's change to it waits there. An active memory is left as it is. Records memory.written with restored. Returns to the memory's own page next= names, its filters kept.
Delete a note POST /console/notes/{id}/delete What notes_delete does, under the file's lock: the note's file and its index rows go for good, and note.written records it with deleted. A plan's narrative (the note a plan:<slug> composition leads with) also needs narrative=<slug> for each plan it narrates, the box beside Delete; without it the delete is refused (409), since a form posts on its first press without script. Refused too while Held holds the note: its file is quarantined, or an agent's change to it waits there. Returns to the Notes list next= names, its filters kept.
Force-release a task claim POST /console/tasks/{id}/release The owner override, Release claim on a task in progress, which asks in the page first on a task's own page, the reading panel and the Tasks list (a lapsed claim's strip on a plan card, Now's loose ends and the Overview's card for one lapsed or claimless claim release at once: no live holder is interrupted): takes the task's claim from whoever holds it, live or lapsed, and tells the holder, or reopens a task marked in progress with no claim at all, so any agent may claim it. Records task.transition with released and by: console. A task no longer in progress has nothing to release: the page says so (a JSON caller gets 409). Not reachable from the agent MCP tools.
Mark a task done, drop it, or reopen it POST /console/tasks/{id}/status Mark done, Drop (which asks in the page first) or Reopen on a task: to=done, dropped or open, through the update tasks_update status= makes, so a closed task unblocks the tasks that depend on it, and the last step of a plan closed as done settles the plan as an agent's close does. Records task.transition with by: console. Refused, naming the holder, while a live claim holds the task: release the claim first. Reopen is for a done or dropped task (one in progress reopens through Release claim); a move to the status the task has writes nothing.
Mark a gate as handled POST /console/tasks/{id}/gate/clear Mark as handled on a task whose own gate is open, with an optional one-line note=: clears the gate as tasks_update gate_clear does, recording the owner as who cleared it and the note. A step's gate clears, and the step goes ahead once nothing else blocks it; a gate closes as done, which unblocks the tasks waiting on it. Records task.transition with gate: cleared and by: console. Refused (409) on a task with no gate, and refused while a live claim holds the task, from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device; a gate already handled writes nothing.
Say what a task waits on POST /console/tasks/{id}/gate Waits on someone on an open or in-progress task whose own gate is not open: who= and what= (one line each), with optional decision= and ready_when=. Sets the task's gate as tasks_update gate_who and gate_what do, so a ready step leaves the ready queue and waits on people until its gate is marked as handled; a gate already cleared opens again. Records task.transition with gate: set and by: console. Refused, naming the holder, while a live claim holds the task, and on a closed task; setting the gate the task already has writes nothing.
Force-release a repo lock POST /console/locks/{id}/release Repo locks: ends the hold a lock carries, live or lapsed, whoever holds it; the lock stays declared. What seam lock release --force sends. Refused when nobody holds it (409), from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Approve a lock declaration POST /console/locks/{id}/approve Makes a restricted account's waiting declaration an active lock, which agents may then hold. With next= a console page (the Overview's Approve), it returns there; a lock decision without one returns to Locks. Refused for a lock already active (409), from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Discard a lock declaration POST /console/locks/{id}/discard Deletes a restricted account's waiting declaration with its repository identities, so the repository may be declared again. An active lock is refused (409): no route removes one. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Approve a captured plan POST /console/plans/{slug}/approve The escape hatch for a Claude Code approval whose PostToolUse never fired: flips the cc-plan note to plan-status:approved and creates the tracking task, exactly as the hook would have. Only applies to a CC capture. ?project=<slug> names the capture's project (every card's Approve sends it); without it the slug's only capture is approved, and a slug captured in two projects is refused (409) with both named. Returns to the plan's page, or with next= a console page (the Overview's Approve, a plan card's) there, with a notice.
Star / unstar an entity POST /console/favorites/{kind}/{id} Toggles the same starred flag the favorite_set MCP tool sets: a starred memory pins into briefings and gets a post-fusion recall boost. For memories and notes the star lives in frontmatter; it never bumps updated. A plan's star is its narrative note's, in the project ?project= names (global for the global scope); without it, the slug's earliest note in any project.
Ask the gardener for proposals POST /console/gardener/request Interprets a natural-language maintenance request into pending proposals. It never mutates a memory.
Plan a project split POST /console/gardener/split Interprets a split request into a plan batch of pending proposals (one split setup plus one reproject per memory). Also never mutates a memory.
Apply one proposal POST /console/gardener/{id}/apply Carries out that proposal's effect. While agents may not apply proposals (Settings, Gardener), this and every other Gardener decision - dismiss, hide, unhide, retarget, undo, dismissing a group, applying a plan - refuse (403) a request from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket and one from a paired device; your browser, your own terminal and the bearer key keep working.
Dismiss a proposal POST /console/gardener/{id}/dismiss Drops it without acting. The pattern is raised again if new evidence for it arrives after the decision.
Hide a proposal forever POST /console/gardener/{id}/hide Drops it without acting and blocks the pattern permanently - no recurrence re-raises it. Listed under Hidden forever.
Unhide a pattern POST /console/gardener/{id}/unhide Lifts a forever block. The proposal stays resolved; the gardener may propose the pattern again the next time it recurs.
Retarget a reproject proposal POST /console/gardener/{id}/retarget Rewrites a pending reproject's destination project before it is applied, and records a gardener.action event with the destination before and after. Reproject proposals only.
Apply a whole plan batch POST /console/gardener/plan/{slug}/apply Applies every pending proposal in a plan, split setup first so the child projects exist before the memories move. Best-effort: it applies what it can, reports how many landed, and leaves the rest pending.
Dismiss a whole rail group POST /console/gardener/group/dismiss Dismisses every pending proposal in one rail section or split plan, one at a time, so each keeps its own event and stays individually undoable. src=you or src=auto narrows a section to the rows the Source filter shows.
Apply a whole rail section POST /console/gardener/group/apply Applies the proposals one rail section shows (group=, and one id= for each proposal shown), one at a time, so each keeps its own event and its own Undo in the decision history. A proposal raised after the page rendered is never applied unseen, and one decided meanwhile is skipped and counted. Offered only on a section whose every proposal can be undone and none of which asks to be read first (it touches a project fenced since it was raised, or moves a stamped memory into a less fenced project); a batch holding any other is refused before anything is applied. A consolidation or a split never takes part. Past that check it is best-effort: it applies what it can, reports how many landed, and leaves the rest pending.
Swap which memory a merge keeps POST /console/gardener/{id}/swap Rewrites a pending merge so it keeps the other memory (keep= names it, one of the two) and retires the one it kept. Nothing changes until the merge is applied. Records a gardener.action event. Merge proposals only.
Undo a decision POST /console/gardener/{id}/undo Returns a resolved proposal to the queue from Recently decided or the decision history, inverting whatever its apply did, for the kinds whose apply can be inverted.
Run a gardener pass now POST /console/gardener/run Runs the background proposal passes now instead of at the next pass, in the background. Like every pass they only propose, except that a new proposal of a kind you turned on under Apply by themselves (gardener.auto_apply, off by default) is applied by the pass that raised it. Refused while a pass runs, while gardener.enabled is false, and where the gardener's schedule is not running on this server.
Release a held write POST /console/held/{id}/release Write screening: lands a held agent write exactly as the agent sent it, and marks the memory owner-confirmed. Refused when its target changed after it was held.
Discard a held write POST /console/held/{id}/discard Lands nothing and erases the held text; the row stays as the record.
Clear a session's outside-text mark POST /console/held/sessions/{id}/clear The only way the mark comes off: the session's changes to binding rules land without a hold again.
Turn lockdown on or off POST /console/held/lockdown on=1 or on=0. Your switch only: a lockdown the configured lockdown file holds stays on until that file goes.
Re-run the review POST /console/held/review Screens every memory and note again and marks the clean ones safe as they read now; your own marks on unchanged items stand.
Mark a flagged item safe POST /console/held/corpus/safe path= the item's file. Safe as it reads now; a memory is also stamped owner-confirmed.
Accept a file changed outside Seamless POST /console/held/corpus/accept path= the file. Records it as it stands, lifts its quarantine, and stamps a memory owner-confirmed.
Set a project's isolation POST /console/projects/{slug}/isolation Changes how far a project's knowledge travels. A tightening that would cut existing context first renders a confirmation step; nothing is written until it is confirmed.
Mark the mishaps reviewed POST /console/mishaps/reviewed Mishaps: Mark reviewed stores when you reviewed the reports, through the newest one the page drew (through= its time; now when absent, never later than now). The Overview's mishap card then counts only the reports after it, and is gone until one arrives. The stamp never moves back: a mark through an older report writes nothing and says so. Records mishaps.reviewed with by: console. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device.
Begin a lock change POST /console/lock/{project}/begin Only under peer_auth, and only from a signed-in browser. action=lock or remove. Refuses first a change that could not apply - a force-locked project, a lock already on, no console lock to remove, a project that is not confidential or sealed, no passkey enrolled - then returns a WebAuthn challenge naming this ceremony, the project and the direction. Writes nothing. A begin never waits for room: at most 4 ceremonies wait at once for one project and direction, and 32 in all, so a begin past 4 displaces the oldest of its project and direction, and one past 32 the oldest of the project and direction holding the most. A displaced ceremony's finish says it expired.
Lock a project, or remove its lock POST /console/lock/{project}/finish Verifies the passkey assertion for that ceremony, then stores the lock or removes it. Turning a lock on ends, in the same transaction, the project's agent leases, read grants and console unlocks, so every agent and browser asks again. It removes only a lock the console set: one peer_auth.force_locked holds stays. Seamless then restarts to apply the change. A finish for a ceremony that began and then failed records access.console_lock_failed under the ceremony's own project and direction, with why: the finish named another project or direction, the passkey's answer did not verify, the passkey is not enrolled, its counter did not increase, another use of it was recorded first, or the project changed since. A finish naming no waiting ceremony records nothing.
Begin a passkey unlock POST /console/unlock/{project}/begin Only for a project peer_auth locks, and only from the signed-in browser that proves its unlock key. Records a waiting console unlock bound to this browser's cookie and key, sets the seamless_unlock cookie when the browser holds no live unlock yet, and returns the passkey challenge. Refused while no passkey is enrolled; the terminal path still works. Opens nothing yet. A begin never waits for room: at most 4 passkey unlocks wait at once for one project, and 32 in all, so a begin past 4 displaces the project's oldest, and one past 32 the oldest of the project holding the most. Terminal unlocks are counted apart.
Unlock a project in this browser POST /console/unlock/{project}/finish Verifies the passkey assertion for that waiting unlock, from the browser that began it, and makes it live: this browser reads the project for three hours, or less when peer_auth.max_lease is shorter. It is never a lease: no agent reads the project through it.
Begin a terminal unlock POST /console/unlock/{project}/terminal Approve from a terminal: the passkey begin's gates, without needing a passkey. Records a waiting unlock bound to this browser and returns a pairing code with the seamlessd console-open --unlock command that approves it, run as the daemon's account within ten minutes. The code only names that unlock, so it is not a secret. Opens nothing until the command runs. Capped as the passkey begin is, apart from it: at most 4 wait for one project, and 32 in all.
Ask for access POST /console/access/request The agent's ask, not your decision: seam access request, run from the agent's own shell, files an access request for a locked project or, with access requests on, what the agent's conversation and a confidential or sealed project no lock covers call for: a grant, or a move into the project. With write=true it asks for a read-and-write grant or a move, a locked project's included, whose approval opens the lock too. It writes a waiting request, with the agent's reason of at most 200 characters, and opens nothing. An agent that already holds the access is answered with it.
Approve an access request POST /console/access/{id}/approve Your decision: writes the agent's lease on a locked project, or a grant, for duration= (until the session ends, 1 hour or 4 hours), and only while the request's facts still match digest=, the digest of the facts you were shown. A grant is read-only unless access=read-write on a request that offers the choice. A move request is approved for good: it ends the conversation's session and opens its continuation in the project, and duration= bounds only a locked project's lock. Under peer_auth it takes a proof: a passkey assertion from the request's page, or a Touch ID signature from Seamless Approve (proof=touchid), accepted on the peer_auth socket only and never for a move. In the advisory tier - access requests without peer_auth - a decision with no passkey is the bearer key's, which is what seam approve sends. A paired device's approval with no passkey or Touch ID proof is refused, peer_auth on or off: the bearer key's decision is never a device's.
Deny an access request POST /console/access/{id}/deny Closes a waiting request with no lease, grant or move; the project stays closed to that agent, and a move's agent stays where it works. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay: deny on the console, or with seam approve in your own terminal on the server.
Revoke an agent's lease POST /console/access/leases/{id}/revoke Revoke on a lease's row under Open right now on /console/access: ends that lease before its expiry and records an access.revoked event. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay.
Revoke a read grant POST /console/access/grants/{id}/revoke Revoke on a grant's row under Open right now on /console/access: ends a live grant, read-only or read and write, before its expiry. Its holder stays write-confined, since a revoke does not unread what it read. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay.
Lock a console unlock again POST /console/access/unlocks/{id}/end Lock again on an unlock's row under Open right now on /console/access, or Lock it again now on the unlock page: ends any browser's live console unlock, by id. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, but for your own hands through a relay.
Begin a passkey enrollment POST /console/approvers/passkey/begin Only under peer_auth: name= the passkey (1 to 64 characters on one line). Returns the WebAuthn creation options, excluding every passkey already enrolled. Holds the enrollment in memory and stores nothing. Refused over the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, since a passkey is created in a browser. A begin never waits for room: at most 16 enrollments wait at once for their browser, and 16 more whose passkey exists and waits for its code, so a begin past 16 displaces the oldest still waiting for its browser, and never one waiting for its code. A displaced enrollment's next step says it expired.
Create the passkey POST /console/approvers/passkey/finish Verifies the browser's new passkey and returns its key's fingerprint with the seamlessd approvers enroll-code command that mints its code. Still stores nothing: the passkey waits for that code. Past 16 waiting for their code, it displaces the oldest of them. Refused from a paired device.
Enroll the passkey POST /console/approvers/passkey/confirm code= the one-time code that command minted for this key. Stores the passkey and uses up the code in one transaction. A code that is mistyped, expired, used or minted for another key leaves the passkey waiting, so it can be typed again. Refused from a paired device.
Enroll a Touch ID key POST /console/approvers/touchid/enroll Seamless Approve's call, from the app seam touchid enroll opens, accepted on the peer_auth socket only - never with the TCP key or the console cookie. Stores the Mac's new Touch ID key, proven by an enrollment code minted for that key and the key's signature over it. An earlier Touch ID key of the same Mac that signs its own retirement is retired in the same step. No console route removes any other credential: that is seamlessd approvers remove.
Begin a passkey sign-in POST /console/signin/begin Only with console.sign_in: passkey, and only from a browser that proves its key (the login page sets it up). Returns the WebAuthn challenge, bound to that key and to a ticket that works once. Writes nothing. A 404 while the key signs browsers in.
Sign in with a passkey POST /console/signin/finish Verifies the assertion for that challenge, from the browser that began it, records the passkey's use, and sets a fresh random sign-in cookie that counts only with this browser's key, for 7 days. A cookie the browser held before ends with it.
Begin adding a passkey POST /console/passkeys/add/begin Only with console.sign_in: passkey: the public Add a passkey page asks for the new passkey's name=. Returns the WebAuthn creation options. Writes nothing.
Add a passkey, waiting POST /console/passkeys/add/finish Verifies the device's new passkey and stores it as waiting, with a short code, for 10 minutes. It adds nothing: seamlessd approvers approve --code, on the server, adds exactly that passkey. It never waits for room: at most 4 wait at once from one address (an IPv6 address counts by its /64, and every loopback address is one), and 32 from every address but loopback, whose 4 are its own. One past its address's 4 displaces that address's oldest, and one past the 32 the oldest of the address holding the most; a displaced passkey's code names nothing, and its page says to add it again. So someone looping on the page from one computer crowds out only their own, and no number of other hosts reaches a passkey added on the server itself. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address.
Begin a terminal sign-in POST /console/signin/terminal/begin Only with console.sign_in: passkey, and only from a browser that proves its key: Show a code for the server's terminal on the login page. Sets a fresh random sign-in cookie bound to that key and stores it waiting, with a short code, for 10 minutes, with the address the request came from and its User-Agent (printable ASCII with each run of spaces as one, at most 256 characters), which the answer also carries for the page to show beside the code. It signs nothing in: seamlessd console-open --sign-in --code, on the server (as the daemon's account under peer_auth, at a terminal), shows those and when it began, asks, and on a yes signs in exactly the browser that showed that code, for 7 days. It never waits for room: at most 4 wait at once from one address (an IPv6 address counts by its /64, and every loopback address is one), and 32 from every address but loopback, whose 4 are its own. A begin past its address's 4 displaces that address's oldest code, and one past the 32 the oldest of the address holding the most; a displaced code approves nothing, and its page says to show a new one. So someone looping on Show a code from one computer crowds out only their own, and no number of other hosts reaches a code a browser on the server itself showed. Behind a proxy every request comes from the proxy's address. A 404 while the key signs browsers in.
Get a pairing code POST /console/devices/code Only on a server that serves other computers (TLS, a bind beyond loopback, or a server_url naming another host). Mints a one-time pairing code, valid for 10 minutes and for one computer, and shows it once, in this answer, with the client one-liners, which carry the server certificate's fingerprint when it serves TLS; only its hash is stored. Without peer_auth the code is the approval; under peer_auth the pairing it starts waits for a passkey. At most 16 codes wait at once. Refused (409, pairing needs TLS here) where the server's address is plain http to another host. Refused (409, server_url names a user) where it names a user. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device, peer_auth on or off.
Begin a device approval POST /console/devices/{id}/approve/begin Only under peer_auth, from a signed-in browser, for a pairing that waits, or for a relay that waits for its approval in place: active, paired with its one-time code alone, and mapped in peer_auth.relays. Returns the WebAuthn challenge, bound to that device's id, kind, name, fingerprint and key (and, in place, to its status and that purpose), and a ticket. Writes nothing.
Approve a device POST /console/devices/{id}/approve/finish Verifies the passkey assertion for that ticket over the device as it stands, records the passkey's use, and pairs the device: a relay's certificate is accepted from its next request, and a key device collects its own key, once, on its next status. A relay waiting in place is approved where it stands, the same device id and certificate, in one compare-and-set that refuses a relay revoked meanwhile; its requests are judged from the next one on, and an access.device_paired event marked in_place records it.
Revoke a device, or deny a pairing POST /console/devices/{id}/revoke Revokes a paired device: its credential is refused from its next request, and the requests it is making end. A pairing that waits is denied instead. Refused from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and from a paired device, peer_auth on or off.
Save briefing settings POST /console/settings/briefing Writes the briefing knobs as a runtime override row in the DB. It never writes the config file.
Reset briefing settings POST /console/settings/briefing/reset Clears the override row, reverting to the file/env configuration.
Preview a briefing POST /console/settings/briefing/preview A read, not a write: it POSTs only to carry the Briefing form's unsaved values, which it checks with the save's own validation, and answers with the briefing a new session in the chosen project would start with. Writes no settings row and records no event. A locked project is not previewed.
Force a project's ranking by use POST /console/settings/utility Knowledge engine's Auto / On / Off on a project's row (or the global scope's, Global context), which saves at once with Undo: sets or clears the owner's per-project force. on and off win over the gardener's readiness latch, auto defers to it again. The answer returns to the row.
Switch embeddings off or back on POST /console/settings/embeddings/mode Stores or clears the embedder off switch. It is read at serve start, so the change applies from the next restart - the page says so.
Re-embed everything POST /console/settings/embeddings/reembed Starts a background pass that re-embeds every memory and note with the active model. It changes vectors, never content.
Choose the console level POST /console/settings/level Stores the experience level as a row that wins over file and env. Presentation only: nothing an agent receives changes.
Reset the console level POST /console/settings/level/reset Clears that row, back to the file/env level.
Dismiss the welcome card POST /console/settings/level/welcome Records that the Overview welcome card was seen, without choosing a level. With the card's write-screening box ticked, it also turns that feature on, as a level choice with the box ticked does.
Save optional features POST /console/settings/features Writes every feature switch as a stored override row in the DB; a switch posts the whole form as soon as it changes. It changes what is exposed - console screens and the matching agent tools - and deletes nothing.
Reset optional features POST /console/settings/features/reset Clears the override row, reverting to the file/env configuration - which, unless you set the keys there, means every optional feature is off again. Still deletes nothing.
Turn update checks on or off POST /console/settings/updates Stores the console's update.check override (check=on or off). It cannot turn checks on while the config file or environment says update.check: false - that is final, and the switch is locked. Off is your decision alone: refused (403) from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket and from a paired device, whatever checks are now; on is open to them. Installs nothing.
Reset update checks POST /console/settings/updates/reset Clears that override - both switches - handing them back to the config file (or, without one, the build's default). A build that is not a published release does not check by default, so there a reset that drops this console's check=on turns checks off, and automatic updates with them: it is refused like turning them off, unless the file or environment locks checks off already. It is refused even where the file's update.check: true would keep them on, since the console cannot see the file's update block under its own override. Every other reset, and every reset on a release build, is open to any caller.
Check for updates now POST /console/settings/updates/check Asks GitHub's release list once, right away - refused while checks are off or within a minute of the last check. Reads; installs nothing.
Turn automatic updates on or off POST /console/settings/updates/auto Stores the console's update.auto override (auto=on or off), keeping its update.check. It cannot turn automatic updates on while the config file or environment says update.auto: false, or locks update.check: false (nothing installs without checks). With checks merely off, the choice is kept and applies once they are back on. Off is your decision alone, refused as turning checks off is; on is open to any caller. Only an install that updates itself acts on it: the installer's, or a peer_auth system daemon's.
Update now POST /console/settings/updates/apply Installs the newest release at once, after a confirm: it skips the soak, the wait for idle agents, skipped releases and the backoff, and lifts a hold, whether automatic updates are on, off or paused. Refused while checks are off, on an install that does not update itself, while an update is under way, within a minute of a failed release check, when nothing newer is known, or when the release carries no signed checksums bundle. The daemon restarts to finish.
Resume automatic updates POST /console/settings/updates/resume Lifts the pause automatic updates put on themselves after rollbacks, and the hold a deliberate downgrade set. Changes no setting; skipped releases stay skipped, and a running backoff runs out.
Save the gardener's switches POST /console/settings/gardener Stores the console's choice for Agents may apply proposals (agents=on or off, over gardener.agents_may_apply; the section's switch sends agents_set=1, with agents=on only while it is on, so its absence is off) or for Apply by themselves (auto_set=1 and one auto=<kind> per kind switched on, over gardener.auto_apply); each control's form carries only its own fields, and each saves the moment a switch changes. It cannot turn agents' applying on while the config file or environment says gardener.agents_may_apply: false - that is final - and it refuses any kind but memory_wanted, tool_error, abandon_plan and ship_plan. Your decision alone in every direction: refused (403) from an agent's process on the peer_auth socket and from a paired device. Applies at once, with no restart; a proposal already waiting is not applied by it. Records a gardener.action event.
Reset the gardener's switches POST /console/settings/gardener/reset Clears that override - both switches - handing them back to the config file, and records a gardener.action event. Refused from an agent's process and from a paired device, as saving is.
Save the backup schedule and folder POST /console/settings/backups Stores the console's backup: override: only the values that differ from the settings in force. A new folder is created and tested with a write first. Applies from the next backup.
Reset the backup settings POST /console/settings/backups/reset Clears that override, handing the schedule and the folder back to the config file (or, without one, the build's default).
Back up now POST /console/settings/backups/now Writes a backup at once, marked Made by you: never skipped, never deleted automatically. With run=retry (the alert card's Try again) it runs the schedule's backup instead, which is skipped when nothing changed and prunes after itself. Refused while a backup runs or a restore is being prepared.
Delete a backup POST /console/settings/backups/delete ref= a backup from the list, never a path. Removes the file from its folder, after a confirm.
Begin a restore's passkey ceremony POST /console/settings/backups/restore/begin Only while peer_auth locks a project, and only from a signed-in browser. Returns a WebAuthn challenge bound to the backup file's SHA-256, which the server reads from the file itself, and to the mode. Writes nothing. A begin never waits for room: at most 4 ceremonies wait at once for one backup and mode, and 32 in all, so a begin past 4 displaces the oldest for its backup and mode, and one past 32 the oldest of the backup and mode holding the most. A displaced ceremony's finish says it expired.
Restore a backup POST /console/settings/backups/restore ref= and mode=replace or merge. Verifies the backup and prepares the restore while Seamless serves, then restarts to finish it. A replace saves today's data as a backup first. Refused while a backup, another restore or an update is under way. Under the passkey gate it also needs the ceremony's id and response, and the file's digest must still match.
Cancel a staged restore POST /console/settings/backups/restore/cancel Drops a restore that is waiting for its restart. Nothing changes.
Dismiss a restore's result POST /console/settings/backups/restore/dismiss Hides the last restore's result card. Changes no data.
Save a project family POST /console/settings/families/save Creates a family or replaces one family's name and member set - the same project_families setting seamlessd family manages. Members come from a closed picker of registered projects, so a typo cannot create an inert member.
Delete a project family POST /console/settings/families/delete Removes the whole family. Its projects lose the sibling-findings channel; nothing else about them changes.
Sign in / sign out POST /console/login, POST /console/logout Sets or clears the console cookie. Touches no data.

Your decisions come through a paired device only as your own hands. On a server that serves other computers, a request that comes with a paired device's credential - a relay's certificate or a device key - is refused (403) on every write that is yours to make: a pairing code and a device's revocation, Held's release, discard, session marks, lockdown and corpus marks, the optional features, turning update checks or automatic updates off (and a reset that would turn checks off), every Backups route, bringing a project's fence down, a deny, a revoke, Lock again, a passkey's enrollment, and an approval with no passkey or Touch ID proof. That holds with peer_auth on or off, with one exception: under peer_auth, a request through a relay you map whose process chain the server judges your own hands there - every process named, none an agent, the chain whole, and your uid there the one both the mapping and the relay's pairing name (the rule) - makes them, and each one it makes records an access.relay_decision event (item: the relay's device; payload: its name, your uid there, the route and the chain's programs by name). Its approval with no passkey or Touch ID proof still goes to the approve core, which refuses it: a chain is no proof. A key device, a relay to a server without peer_auth, and any other chain carry their agents, never your hands, and the refusal says why: make these decisions in the console of the server you sign in to, in a terminal on the server itself, or in a terminal of your own behind a relay you map. The reads stay open to a device, and so do the writes an agent may make: seam on a client computer reads the console's JSON through its relay, and the Touch ID helper there approves through it with its own signature.

Read the shape of that list. There is no "create memory", no "edit note", no "delete memory", no "add task", no "start session". The direct writes to knowledge state are archive and restore a memory, delete a note, approve a captured plan, the star flag, and - with write screening on - releasing a held write, which lands exactly what an agent wrote, never text of the console's own; the rest either manage gardener proposals - which are themselves proposals, reviewed before they do anything - or move a task the way tasks_update does (release its claim, mark it done, drop or reopen it, mark its gate as handled or say what it waits on), or record a decision about the work (a repo lock's declaration or hold, a project's isolation, the mishaps marked reviewed), or set a configuration knob (briefing overrides, feature switches, project families, the update switches, the gardener's switches, the backup schedule and folder) that shapes future briefings, what is exposed, or how the install runs, without touching any memory's content. Back up now and Delete a backup make and remove copies of the data, never the data itself. The console level is presentation state of the same kind: it changes what this console shows you and nothing else. The access, lock, unlock and approver rows exist only with peer_auth or access requests on (both optional, and off by default; every one of those routes answers 404 otherwise), and they are your decisions about who may reach a project, not writes to knowledge: they record requests, leases, grants, moves (a move ends the conversation's session and opens its continuation in the project it moved into), console unlocks, locks and approver credentials, and never a memory's or a note's content. The one an agent calls, Ask for access, only files a request for you to decide. Update now and Resume automatic updates act on the install rather than on knowledge: the first starts the same backed-up update seamlessd update runs, the second lets automatic updates run again. A restore is the one write that changes knowledge wholesale, and it puts back what a backup of this install held, never text of the console's own: the data from before is saved as a backup first, so a restore is itself undone by restoring.

This is deliberate, and it is the same principle as the gardener's propose-only default. The store is written by agents doing work, with provenance attached. A console that could quietly edit a memory would produce knowledge that came from nowhere, attributable to no session, explaining nothing.

Every write action redirects back with a flash message (?notice= for success, ?error= for failure) rather than rendering a result page in place, so a reload never repeats the action. With script, a success notice surfaces as a toast and both parameters are stripped from the address bar, so a later live refresh never replays a message about an action that already happened; an error also stays on the page as a banner.

Signing in

There is one credential in the whole system: the static bearer key (mcp.api_key). It guards /api/mcp, the hook endpoints, and the console alike.

Two ways to present it:

  • A browser trades the key for a cookie at /console/login. The cookie value is a SHA-256 hash of the key, not the key - so the raw credential never sits in the browser's cookie jar. It is HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, and scoped to /console. The login page is one card: the key's field and Sign in, with Where is my key? folded under it (the config file that holds the key, SEAMLESS_MCP_API_KEY, and seamlessd console-open, which opens the console already signed in).
  • The seam CLI sends the key as a bearer token on the Authorization header, and asks for JSON.

Unauthenticated browsers are redirected to the login page with a ?next= that is validated against an open-redirect (an off-site or absolute candidate becomes /console/). Unauthenticated JSON callers get a 401.

Public routes are the login page, the static assets (console.css, interactions.js, search.js, favicon.svg and the rest under /console/static/) and the service worker at /console/sw.js. Everything else requires the key.

A browser sends its cookies to every port of the same host, so a program that can open your browser on another local port receives the console cookie too. Today that adds nothing to what reading the key gives such a program. A console unlock of a locked project is worth more, and so is a passkey sign-in, so neither is just a cookie: each also needs a key the browser keeps for the console's own address, and a service worker signs each console request with that key. The service worker runs in a browser that has started an unlock, and under passkey sign-in in every signed-in browser. Before an unlock or a sign-in the page asks the daemon for the worker again, and when an upgrade brought a new one, it waits while the new worker takes over, so the old one never signs for the new daemon. The worker and its key script (/console/static/browserkey.js) are served no-cache, so the browser checks with the daemon each time it loads them. The other static files are linked by version (After an upgrade).

Sign in with a passkey

Set console.sign_in: passkey in the daemon's config (off by default; file only) and restart it, and a browser signs in with a passkey you added, in any browser, the server's included. No browser needs the key: the login page no longer takes it, and a cookie derived from it signs nothing in. The seam CLI keeps sending the key.

The sign-in page keeps its sky, and its right column is one card: Sign in with a passkey, how long a sign-in lasts (its hint says which passkeys work here), then under "no passkey here?" the two other ways in, Show a code for the server's terminal and Add a passkey on this device.

  • Signing in. The login page sets up the browser's key and service worker, then asks for your passkey: this device's, one your password manager syncs here, or your phone's through the browser's QR prompt. The daemon answers with a random cookie and keeps only a hash of it and the browser's key together, so the cookie read on another port opens nothing. A sign-in lasts 7 days in that browser, or until you sign out from the sidebar (which also drops its console unlocks), or until the passkey that made it is removed. A restore signs every browser out.
  • A page drawn without the proof (a hard reload skips the worker) lands on the login page, which sets the worker up and asks for the page again. A browser that cannot run a service worker (some private windows) cannot sign in.
  • Adding a passkey for a new device. On the server, seamlessd approvers add prints the Add a passkey address (/console/passkeys/add on the passkey origin). It is not a secret: anyone who reaches the console can open it, and nothing is added until you approve. Open it on the device and create the passkey; the page shows a short code and the key's fingerprint. Run seamlessd approvers approve --code 7KQ2-M9XD on the server (as the daemon's account under peer_auth; the page shows the exact command). It shows the same name and key and asks before it adds, so it runs only at a terminal (over ssh, ssh -t), and no flag skips the question. Approve only a code your own device shows.
  • No passkey at hand. Show a code for the server's terminal, under "no passkey here?", begins a terminal sign-in: the browser gets a cookie bound to its key and shows, as steps, the code, the command that approves it and what that command will show of this browser, /usr/bin/sudo -k -u _seamless /usr/bin/env SEAMLESS_CONFIG=/opt/seamless/etc/seamless.yaml /opt/seamless/bin/seamlessd console-open --sign-in --code 7KQ2-M9XD under peer_auth (seamlessd console-open --sign-in --code 7KQ2-M9XD without it). Approved, that browser is signed in for 7 days, as with a passkey, and the page goes on by itself. The command first shows the browser the code names (when it began, its address and User-Agent) and asks; say yes only to a code your own browser shows you now. The code signs in no other browser, so reading it off your screen gives nothing away. It is the way back in when every passkey is lost: add a new one from the Add a passkey page.
  • Synced passkeys. A passkey synced through iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager or another password manager is one passkey: add it once, and every device it syncs to signs in, with nothing more to add. A device without it can use your phone's passkey through the browser's QR prompt.
  • The server's name. A passkey works only for the name it was made for. One made for another site, or for localhost on another install, does not work here. With localhost passkeys only a browser on the server itself can make or use one. Renaming the server, or turning TLS off, strands every passkey made for the old name (doctor names them).

Approvers

Under peer_auth, /console/approvers lists the passkeys and Touch ID keys that approve: one card per key, with what it is (a passkey, a synced passkey, or Touch ID in the agent's dialog), when it was last used and the day it was added. A key's hint (its three dots) holds its id and the command that removes it, run in your own terminal as the daemon's account. The page never removes a key: the console's key is no proof of you.

Add one offers two tiles. A passkey takes three steps: name it and create it in this browser, make its one-time code in your own terminal (the page shows the command, with Copy; the code enrolls only the passkey you just created), then enter the code. Touch ID on a Mac is seam touchid enroll, with Copy. Under passkey sign-in a passkey is added from the device that will hold it, so the passkey tile links the Add a passkey page and the command that approves its code instead. With passkeys off, or on an address that is not the passkey origin, the tile says so. The Add a passkey page walks the same way in three steps: create it there, approve its code on the server, sign in with it.

make console

make console          # open in the default browser, already signed in
make console-chrome   # same, but force Google Chrome

This builds, then runs seamlessd console-open, which renders a one-shot self-submitting login page to a 0600 temp file and opens it. The page POSTs the key to /console/login, which sets the cookie and 303s into the console - so you land on an authenticated page with nothing to paste. It refuses to run if mcp.api_key is empty or the server is not answering /healthz. Under passkey sign-in, console-open opens the sign-in page instead and writes no page and no key.

make console-chrome exists for agents: they drive Chrome, so this hands the auth cookie to the browser they can actually see. (--browser is macOS-only.)

Getting around

The sidebar groups the screens by the job they serve rather than by table, in this order:

Group Screens
Access Access requests, Approvers (only while peer_auth locks a project; Access requests alone while read grants are on). Whenever it exists it is the first group: a waiting request is an agent waiting on you.
Live Overview, Now, Interactions, Mishaps
Work Diary (only while that optional feature is on), Projects, Plans, Tasks, Sessions, Locks (only while that optional feature is on)
Knowledge Memories, Notes, Retrieval, Gardener, Held (only while write screening is on, or restricted accounts are configured)
Research Labs, Trials (only while that optional feature is on)
Server System, Privacy, Devices (only on a server that serves other computers)

That is the full list, at the Advanced level; a lower level shows a subset, in the same order and under the same names. Above the groups, a Search or jump to field opens the command palette; Settings and the account row (the server the console runs on, by its machine name, the theme, sign out) close the sidebar. Only the groups scroll, with a fade at an edge that has more beyond it, so the search field, Settings and the account row stay on screen at any window height. The sidebar collapses to an icon rail (the header button, or [) and remembers that per browser; under 720px it becomes a drawer behind the menu button, with every section's label and badge.

A number beside a section is one of two kinds:

Kind Sections Shows
Waiting on you Access requests, Mishaps (reports since you last marked them reviewed), Plans (captured plans awaiting your approval), Tasks (gates waiting on you, lapsed claims, and tasks in progress with no claim), Locks (declarations waiting for your approval), Gardener (proposals waiting for review), Held A pill while something waits, and nothing at zero. Each counts what the Overview's matching Needs you cards count.
Live Now The agents live right now, dimmed at zero.

The other sections carry no number: their totals are on the Overview and at the head of each screen. On the collapsed rail a section with something waiting carries a dot on its icon, and on a phone the menu button carries one while anything in the drawer waits. The badges follow the live refresh like the rest of the page.

Every screen title carries an (i) button that says, in one line, what the screen is for.

Read in place

A plain click on a link to a memory, a note, a task, a plan, a session, an event or a trial opens it in a wide panel over the page. The page stays as it was behind it: never reloaded, its scroll and open folds kept, its live updates going on. A click on a row of Sessions, Search, Mishaps, the Tasks list or a project's tabs does the same. A project link still opens the project.

  • The panel's header says where the item lives (its project, then Memories, Notes, Tasks and so on, or a task's plan:<slug>), with k and j for the previous and next item of the list it was opened from, Open full page, and Esc Close. On a phone it takes the whole screen.
  • Esc, Close, a click beside the panel or the browser's Back closes it, and focus goes back to the link that opened it. A link inside the panel opens that item in it, a step that Back takes back.
  • The address carries #peek= and the item, so a reload opens the panel again.
  • An action inside it (Mark done, the star, Archive and the rest) applies there: its message shows, and the panel shows the item as it is now, or closes when the item is gone (a deleted note). The page behind catches up through its live refresh.
  • A Cmd/Ctrl-click, a middle click, or a link from outside the console (an agent's message, a new tab) opens the item's own page. When you go there from a console page (Open full page), its way back reads Back to that page's title and returns there.
  • The Diary and Interactions keep the pane they open beside the day or the feed.

Hints, switches that save at once, and time left

Settings and the lock screens share a few parts.

  • A hint is a small (i) beside the thing it explains. It opens on hover, on keyboard focus, or with a tap, which pins it open on a phone. Esc, a tap outside it, or opening another hint closes it, so one is open at a time, and an Esc that closes a hint leaves open what lies under it. Its words are in the page: a screen reader reads them with the button.
  • A switch that saves at once posts as soon as it changes, through the same in-place path as every other console write, and waits, disabled, for Seamless to answer. The toast then names the change ("Momentum is off.") with Undo, which posts the values from before it. A save that fails puts the switch back and says why, with Try again. Typing never saves: a form with a typed value (a number, a folder) keeps its Save bar. A toast with a button stays for eight seconds, and for as long as the pointer or focus is on it.
  • Time left on a lease, a grant or an unlock reads "2 h 41 m left". It counts down every 30 seconds while the page is in sight, turns amber from 30 minutes, when renewal warnings start, and stops at ended. Its tooltip is the end, in your own clock. A lease with no end of its own reads until the session ends.
  • Steps list a ceremony with more than one step, each done (a check), the one under way, or still to come, numbered: a restore's progress in Backups is one.
  • The source chip in a Settings section's head says where its values come from: Config file, Set here with Reset, or Config file decides with a lock when the config file makes a value final. Its hint says more.

The command palette

Cmd/Ctrl+K, the sidebar's search field, or / on a screen with no filter of its own opens the palette. With nothing typed it offers Recent (the memories, notes, tasks, plans, sessions, projects, labs and trials you last opened in this browser, by their titles; an event page is never kept), Jump to (every section the sidebar offers, with its shortcut, plus Search, Context, and each Settings section the level shows), and Actions (switch theme, collapse the sidebar, the shortcut sheet, change the experience level, and, while the level shows Privacy, lock a project: Privacy's Locked card). Typing matches sections and actions instantly; from two characters on it also searches memories, notes, tasks, plans, trials, projects, and sessions through the same route as Search, showing the groups the level offers. Each group shows up to five, starred matches first and marked starred; a group with more shows its count as 5+ and ends with More in Search, which opens Search narrowed to that kind. An exact name of a superseded or archived memory finds it here too, with its status.

Keyboard

Keys Does
Cmd/Ctrl+K Search or jump to a section
/ Focus this screen's filter; open the palette where there is none
g then a key Go to a section (pressing g shows every key it can take, until your next key, Esc or a click): a Access requests, k Approvers, o Overview, n Now, i Interactions, f Mishaps, d Diary, w Projects, p Plans, t Tasks, s Sessions, b Locks, m Memories, e Notes, r Retrieval, g Gardener, h Held, l Labs, x Trials, y System, v Privacy, c Devices, , Settings
j / k Next / previous item in a library rail (Gardener, Labs, Trials), the Memories list, the Notes list or the Tasks list, or, on an item's own page, in the list it is in
Enter On the Memories, Notes or Tasks list, open the focused row's own page
p Open the project switcher on Memories, Notes, Tasks and Plans
a / x On the Gardener: apply / dismiss the open proposal. An apply that cannot be undone asks in the page first; press a again to confirm
[ Collapse or expand the sidebar
? The shortcut sheet
Esc / k / j In the reading panel: close it / the previous / the next item of the list it was opened from
Esc Close the palette, a menu, a hint, the sheet, or the drawer

The g map is read from the sidebar itself, so a section switched off in Settings - or one the level leaves out of the sidebar - takes its shortcut with it, and brings it back when it returns.

Moving between screens keeps the sidebar in place and settles the new content in (cross-document view transitions, where the browser supports them), and hovering a console link prefetches its page. Neither runs any code of the destination page early; both degrade to a plain navigation.

Ambient signals

The console shows activity without asking to be read. The line along the sidebar's edge - the Seam - carries each event from the live stream as a spark that travels to the section it belongs to and lights that section's icon: cyan for context reaching an agent, green for knowledge written, coral for something wrong, indigo for everything else. Each event also rings the daemon's dot in the sidebar and the page's live dots once, and the sky behind the pages brightens with the recent event rate and settles when the fleet is idle; the dot dims while the live stream is down. Headline numbers count up when a page opens; agents working right now carry a slow orbit of light on the Now screen. The page settling in and the count-up play once per browser tab, on the first page it shows; later pages in that tab appear at once.

All of it is decoration over data the page already states: nothing here changes a number, and prefers-reduced-motion stills every part of it (the Seam sends no sparks, numbers render at their value). Between events the sky and the sidebar hold still, so a console left open on the Overview draws nothing while the fleet is idle.

After an upgrade

Every page links its stylesheet and scripts by their version, a digest of the file this build serves (/console/static/console.css?v=...). The browser keeps each one until a build changes it, so the first page load after an upgrade uses the new stylesheet and scripts, and loads after that fetch none of them again. A static file asked for without its version, such as the worker's import of browserkey.js, is checked with the daemon on each use.

A tab left open across an upgrade keeps the stylesheet and scripts it loaded first while its views update in place. When the daemon now serves different ones, the page says so once, in the corner: "Seamless was updated. Reload this page to use the new version." The console never reloads the page itself; Reload does, when you choose.

Choose how much you see

The console has three experience levels. They change what the console shows you and nothing else: your agents get the same briefing, the same MCP tools, the same hooks, the same recall, and the same gardener at every level. The level is presentation, stored for this installation's owner rather than per browser, so your phone and your laptop agree.

Basic is the essentials, for someone who installed Seamless because they use Claude Code or Codex and wants to know it works: the work the agents follow (Projects, Plans, Tasks), what they did (Sessions) and what went wrong (Mishaps), what they remember (Memories, Notes), cleanup suggestions to accept or decline (Gardener), and an Overview whose health strip, right under what needs you, says which agent clients are working here, whether semantic recall is on, when the last briefing went out, and the version (which says when a newer release is out) - plus the Experience, Features, Your setup, Updates, Backups and Gardener settings.

Standard adds watching the agents live and looking after the server: Now (and Locks, and Labs and Trials, when their features are on), System and Privacy, the Overview's window, vitals, and projects table, the Briefing and Workspaces settings, and the finer controls on the screens Basic already had.

Advanced is every screen and every knob: Interactions (the tool-call transport), Retrieval (the analytics), Context, the Knowledge engine settings, and raw event payloads.

A fresh installation starts at Basic, and Home carries a one-time welcome card offering all three - pick one, or dismiss it; either way it does not come back, on any device. Beside the levels the card offers one optional feature as an unchecked box, Also turn on write screening: it rides with whichever button you press, and unticked it changes nothing at any level. It is a feature, not part of a level, because it changes what your agents receive (see Held); once the card is gone, Settings > Features is the way in. Settings > Experience shows the level you are on, with the three levels side by side and the list of what each one shows. The palette's Change experience level action goes there too.

Hidden, not locked. A level removes screens from the sidebar, the palette, and the shortcut map; it never locks them. A link to a screen above your level - from these docs, an agent's finding, a briefing, a bookmark - still opens it, under a note saying it is not in your sidebar, with a button to switch; Got it sets the note aside for that screen in this browser. JSON callers (?format=json, and so the seam CLI, seam doctor included) get the same answer at every level.

Upgrading keeps every screen. An installation that already recorded sessions before levels existed is set to Advanced by a one-time upgrade step, so nothing you were using disappears; Settings > Experience says the level was set by the upgrade, and the welcome card appears once to announce the choice.

Levels and optional features compose: a screen shows when its feature is on and the level includes it. Features change what exists - for the console and for agents alike; the level only changes how much of it you see. The level can also come from the config file or environment (console.level, SEAMLESS_CONSOLE_LEVEL) - a choice made in the console wins until you reset it there. See Configuration.

Three ways to render a page

Every route answers in the shape the caller asked for:

  • HTML by default - the full page, layout and all.
  • JSON when the caller sets ?format=json or an Accept header that wants JSON and not HTML. This is how seam reads the console's data.
  • An HTML fragment for entity details when the caller passes ?peek=1 - the reading panel (or the Diary's or Interactions' pane) loads it without a page navigation - or ?reader=1, the richer reader fragment the screens that keep a rail and a reader (Gardener, Labs, Trials) swap in place. A memory, a note, a task and a plan answer ?reader=1 too.

The event page composes its full page from the same detail-body block its peek fragment renders, so the two cannot drift. Session and project deliberately do not: their fragments are compact summaries of much richer bespoke pages. Lab and trial detail URLs, and a gardener proposal's (/console/gardener/{id}), render their screen with that entity open in the reader; a memory, a note, a task and a plan open on their own page.

Strictly-validated query params (?sort, ?scope, ?tab, ?w) return a 400 naming the bad param and listing the valid values, rather than silently falling back to a default - so an agent driving the console by URL sees the fix.

GET /console/events is the SSE stream: every recorded event as one JSON data: frame, with a ping every 25 seconds. A retrieval.injected frame also lists the memories it surfaced as itemIds (capped at 48), which is what lets a page point at exactly what reached an agent. ?feed=interactions opts into the richer transport-level rows the Interactions screen consumes. A console tab holds its stream only while you can see it: 10 seconds after it goes out of sight (a background tab or a minimized window) it lets the stream go, because a browser opens only a few connections to a console served over plain http (six in Chrome) and each open stream keeps one. Shown again, it opens the stream again and refreshes once to catch up (the Interactions feed fills in the rows it missed), and a live refresh with no answer after 15 seconds gives up and leaves the tap-to-refresh pill. Under peer_auth the stream leaves out every event about a locked project this browser has not unlocked, with one exception: an agent's access request for one arrives as its kind, id and time alone, so the open page refreshes its Access requests count.

A live refresh changes the page without a word; only a refresh you ask for with the pill says Updated. Three events also raise a toast that links to the screen that acts on them: an agent asking for access (Access requests), a write held for review (Held) and a reported mishap (Mishaps).

Overview

/console/

The check-in page. It answers what waits on you first, then what is in motion, then whether stored knowledge is reaching your agents. Top to bottom:

  • The level chooser - on a fresh installation, the one-time welcome card (see Choose how much you see).
  • Needs you - one card per thing that waits on you, most urgent first. The number beside the heading is how many items the cards stand for, their counts added up (a card for 36 gates counts 36), plans at the finish line aside; hover it for how many cards that is. First what an agent is blocked on right now: access requests waiting for you (while a project is locked or access requests are on), writes held for your review (with write screening on, or restricted accounts' proposals), lock declarations waiting for you (with repo locks on), open gates waiting on you (then gates waiting on someone else, named), captured plans presented and awaiting your approval, claims that lapsed, and tasks marked in progress with no claim. Then your own queues: mishaps to review, an update that failed, rolled back or paused itself, and backups that are failing, stopped, missing, or older than a week. Then the knowledge queue: gardener proposals, what automatic apply applied, memories going stale, and, with momentum on, plans at the finish line. Each card is one sentence with its count and a link to the screen that answers it; a card for a screen your level does not show names it without a link. Where one step settles a card, that step is on it - Mark as handled for one gate, Approve for one plan or one lock declaration, Release claim for one lapsed or claimless claim - posting to the same route the task, plan or lock page posts to, and coming back here: the strip redraws in place, without a reload. Access requests and held writes are decided on their own pages (an approval is a passkey ceremony; a held write is read first). A card whose optional feature is off does not exist.
  • Agent-reported mishaps - the mishap card counts every report since you last marked them reviewed on the Mishaps screen (every report before your first review), at the true count, names the latest report's type, age and project, and opens the Mishaps screen. Mark reviewed there clears it until a new report arrives.
  • Going stale - the knowledge card counts the active memories with no update, injection, or read in gardener.staleness_days (90 days by default, the gardener's own staleness horizon), exactly the rows Retrieval's quiet-knowledge list shows, states the horizon, and opens that list. Changing the setting moves the card, the list and their labels together.
  • Work in motion - the model Now draws, as one row: the plans a live claim holds a step of, with the agents holding them; the loose ends (in progress, but no live agent carries them); and what an agent could claim next, three of each with their true counts.
  • Live now - up to six live agents, each led by the task it holds with a live claim, else by its project, then how many more, and All N live to Now.
  • Vitals (Standard and up) - see below - closed by the health line.
  • Recently active projects (Standard and up) - the top projects by recent activity, drawn from the same batched query the Projects board uses, so a row here reconciles with a row there exactly, beside the most reused knowledge.
  • Knowledge sky - a star chart of every active memory, with no cap, below the projects. Fold puts it away; this browser remembers, and a folded sky stays folded on every visit. Each project (and the global scope) owns a wedge sized by its share of memories, largest first. Distance from the centre is when the memory last surfaced to an agent: the core holds the last 24 hours, rings mark 7 days and the staleness horizon, gardener.staleness_days (90 days by default; the same fresh and stale lines the memory reader's "since surfaced" chip uses), and the rim belt holds memories that have never surfaced. Colour is kind; size is demand (the query-gated utility score, so a big star is one agents pull, not one the briefing merely shows). Hollow stars have never surfaced, a ring marks a starred memory, spikes mark one written today, and today's stars twinkle as the chart appears. Beside the chart, a readout states the same picture as text: each ring's count, the going-stale count (memories with no update, injection, or read within the staleness horizon: always the stale card's count and the rows Retrieval's quiet-knowledge list shows), and, under Projects, every project with its ring mix as a bar. Point at a star for its name and description (the pointer snaps to the nearest star); click it for a card with its facts and a link to open it; double-click to open it directly. Type in Find a memory to light only the matches (name, description, tag, project, or kind) and list them, with the arrow keys and Enter to step through; click a ring, the going- stale line, a project, or a kind chip to filter the same way, and point at one to preview it. When an injection or a read lands on the live stream, each memory it names sends a beam into the core, and the refresh that follows glides the star to its new ring; a newly written memory appears with a flare. A star keeps its place while its project and ring are unchanged, and the rings and wedges resize in steps rather than with every memory, so a refresh moves only what changed, and search, filters, and the selection survive it. The refresh downloads only what changed, too: the stars that changed, arrived, or left since the chart the page holds, and nothing of the sky when nothing in it did. It is HTML only - the JSON answer carries no sky.
  • Recent activity - the latest events, each linking to its detail page.

At Basic the health line comes right after the cards: which agent clients are working here, whether semantic recall is on, when the last briefing went out, a warning while there is no backup or the newest is older than a week, and the version.

The four judged vitals (memory reach, knowledge continuity, context injections, sessions reached) are drill-down links carrying the selected window: reach, injections, and sessions reached land on the Retrieval screen whose hero and delivery funnel are the same numbers over the same report, and continuity lands on the Sessions list filtered to ?retained=no - the sessions that kept nothing. An empty-state card stays linked, because the destination explains why there is nothing. Below Advanced, where Retrieval is not in the sidebar, the three Retrieval vitals are plain cards.

No link above your level. A link whose screen your level's sidebar does not show - Locks and Now at Basic, Retrieval and Interactions below Advanced - is not offered as a link anywhere on this page: the card, the row or the count says the same thing as plain text. The screen still opens by URL, under the level note.

Live sessions are counted TTL-aware (active and heartbeated within the idle threshold, or holding a live claim), so the headline matches the Sessions screen rather than the raw active count that an idle session inflates until the reaper runs.

?format=json answers the page's model at every level: Attention is the needs-you list, each item with its Kind (a stable key: access, held, lock-declarations, gates, gates-others, plan-approval, claims-lapsed, claims-unclaimed, mishaps, updates, backups, proposals, auto-applied, stale, finish-line), Count, Title, Sub, Href, Blocking when an agent is blocked on it, and its Action (the route it posts and its fields) when one step settles it; Motion is Work in motion; Live, LiveTotal and LiveMore are the live strip.

Since you were last here

When you come back to the Overview after at least five minutes away, a line under the cards answers the check-in question -- what changed while I was gone? -- with counts: memories written, sessions started, tasks closed, notes written, gardener proposals raised, and mishaps reported since you last looked ("Quiet since you were last here 3h ago" when nothing was recorded). Each count links its screen - the mishaps count the Mishaps screen

  • where your level shows it.

"Last looked" is a per-browser stamp, set whenever a console tab is hidden or left; the counts come from GET /console/since?t=<unix ms>, which answers JSON only and refuses a missing, malformed, future, or older-than-90-days t with a 400 rather than substituting a window.

Now

/console/now

The exploded live view: what every agent is doing right now, across every project and plan at once. Where the project workspace is task-centric, Now is agent-centric - the unit is the live session, and everything it holds rides its card. The sidebar entry's badge is the live agent count, and the page refreshes on every event kind (tool calls included - here they are the signal, not noise), morphing in place like every other screen.

Top to bottom:

  • The titlebar - live agent count and the fleet-wide pulse: an events-per- five-minutes sparkline over the last hour, all kinds, deliberately unfiltered by project.
  • A project strip - all, then one chip per project with a live agent (?scope=<slug>; the global scope filters as global). Filtering narrows every zone except the pulse.
  • On duty - one card per live session, headed by the title of the task it holds, else by its first prompt as the Sessions screen titles its rows, else by its session name, with the session name, harness+model pill and account under it; then its project, when it was last seen (cards are toned hot/warm/quiet by heartbeat age), how long it has been running, cumulative tokens, a star toggle, every claim it holds with a live lease countdown, and a short trail of what it just produced. A claim it let lapse reads on its card as it reads in Loose ends: "claim lapsed 12m ago:" and the task's title. A live agent holding nothing says so: "holds no claim".
  • Loose ends - in_progress tasks no live agent is carrying: a lapsed lease, a claimless start (tasks_update status=in_progress without a claim), or a holder that went quiet mid-lease. Each row says its state once, in the words every task screen uses: "claim lapsed 12m ago", "unclaimed", or "in progress" with the quiet holder named and its lease counting down. A lapsed claim offers release claim with no confirmation - the lease is already dead, so there is no live holder to interrupt, only a stale claim to clear.
  • Plans moved in 24h - a horizontally scrolling rail of every incomplete plan across every project, done/in-flight progress bars and ready counts, headed by how many moved in the last 24 hours, cards dimmed once a plan has rested for 24h. Each links to its plan's page, or, for a plan with no narrative note in its project, to that project's Plans & tasks tab (the Plans board for the global scope).
  • Up next - the cross-project ready queue: claimable this instant, plan steps included, each naming what closing it would unblock.
  • The wire - the freshest business events, filtered by the project strip.

Everything links onward - sessions, tasks, plans, projects, events - and the lease countdowns tick client-side between refreshes. A title wraps to two lines rather than cutting at one, and one that two lines still cut keeps its whole text on hover. With the gamification feature on, the page also carries the day tape, the personal-records rail, the hot-streak pulse, and celebration moments; off (the default), none of that renders.

Interactions

/console/interactions

The clean live feed of what agents are actually doing: MCP tool calls, hook injections, recall-miss prompts, session lifecycle, and the plan-mode capture stream. A fresh page opens with the five newest interactions, under a Before you arrived divider, and listens from that moment forward.

Older history is explicit and additive. Choose a recent window and select Add when earlier context is useful; live rows stay in place, and Load older events paginates only inside that chosen window. Loaded history sits under a Before you arrived divider, with what arrived live above it. The empty feed offers the window you loaded last time in this browser as its first button, and the other windows beside it; that choice is kept in this browser only and never loads by itself. Filters operate over the rows already in memory, by event category and session lane. Pausing buffers new arrivals rather than discarding them.

Each compact row expands just enough to expose its request/result or injected text. Selecting the inspector keeps that context beside the stream and links to the full event page. A recall via the MCP tool records both a retrieval.injected and a tool.call; the injected twin is dropped here because the tool call carries the same content plus its arguments. Session lifecycle twins are kept on purpose, as feed markers.

Search

/console/search

One query across every entity the console can link to. Memories and notes come through the same fused FTS + semantic retrieval that recall uses, with snippets; tasks, plans, trials, projects, and sessions have no FTS mirror and match by LIKE.

Counts are honest. Each kind shows up to 20 results and is fetched one further, so a kind with more says so: its count reads 20+ and its Show more opens up to 200 of that kind (?more=tasks, comma-separated for several). Show more is part of the address, so it survives the live refresh and the Type, Updated, Starred, Archived, and Sort controls; a new query starts with it closed. A kind still cut at 200 says how many it shows and asks for a narrower search. The header's total carries the same + when any kind was cut. Memories and notes are counted apart, so many matching memories never squeeze the notes out.

Each kind wears one color wherever Search names it: its count in the results header ("1 Session", "2 Sessions") is the legend for its rows, and the Type filter, the palette's group heads and an empty page's type chip carry the same color as a dot. Archived and superseded memories wear a quieter take of the memory color.

Starred only (?fav=1) runs inside each query, before the cut, so a starred match ranked past the first 20 still appears. Without it, a kind's starred matches take its first slots, then the best of the rest.

Superseded and archived memories, which every other search leaves out, have their own lookup here. An exact memory name or ID always finds one, under Archived & superseded, badged superseded (with a link to the memory that replaced it) or archived. Include archived (?archived=1, offered while memories are in scope) finds them by text as well. A locked project's retired memories stay out, like the rest of its content.

A one-character query says to type at least two characters. A query that finds nothing lists each restriction in force - the type, the Updated window, Starred only - as a chip that removes it, with Clear all filters when there are two or more; when archived or superseded memories match where nothing live does, it says how many and offers Include archived.

Stable references get their own lookup lane. An exact memory name or note slug ranks ahead of token-overlap matches and is shown beside the result's display title. A full memory, note, task, session, or trial ULID works case-insensitively; an 8-character-or-longer ULID prefix finds every match of those kinds without letting a short prefix such as 01 flood the page. Identifier matches keep the canonical ID-based detail link and are labeled separately from keyword and semantic matches.
