The command palette (⌘K, available on every page) fetches this same route with ?format=json&fast=1, which drops the semantic leg - a query per keystroke must never cost a remote embedding round-trip.

The semantic leg is nearest-neighbor: there is always a "nearest" memory, however far, so a semantic-only hit must clear search.semantic_floor (cosine similarity, default 0.3) to appear - without the floor any query, including nonsense, would fill the page to its limit. A hit the keyword leg also matched is exempt. Every hit the semantic leg found shows its similarity as a percentage, so you can see where relevance falls off; keyword-only hits show a highlighted snippet instead. Agent-facing recall applies no floor - an agent can judge a weak hit for itself.

Coverage is deliberately partial in one place: events are excluded because the telemetry stream has its own Interactions surface and would flood results.

Diary

/console/diary, /console/diary?day=YYYY-MM-DD

Only while the Diary optional feature is on. Then it shows at every level, as the first row of the sidebar's Work group, and g then d opens it. It is a page for each day of work: what was worked on, which agents did it, and what it took in agent time and model tokens, with the meaningful work in the spotlight and short question-and-answer sessions folded away. A day runs from midnight to midnight in the daemon's time zone, so a daylight-saving day has 23 or 25 hours. The page is composed from what Seamless already records (the usage ledger, the event log, the sessions, tasks, memories, notes, trials and commit records), by stated rules and no model.

/console/diary is today; ?day= is another day, and &m=YYYY-MM shows another month in the rail beside it. A day or m that does not parse is a 400 that names the format.

What a day shows

The date block. The weekday, the date, and the day's character as a stamp whose tooltip states its rule. The character is the first of these the day meets:

Character Rule
Quiet No session, task or item recorded
Shipped A plan shipped: its last open step closed as done
Closing day 5 or more tasks closed as done
Planning day A plan drafted (captured, presented or approved) or 6 or more tasks created, and fewer than 2 closed
Deep work 2h or more of agent time, 60% or more of it in one project
Busy day 3h or more of agent time, 12 or more sessions beyond the short ones, or work in 4 or more projects
Light day Work recorded, under every threshold of a fuller day

Under it, the headline: "Mostly X: ..." when one thing took at least half the day's agent time (or was the only thing worked on), "Led by X: ..." otherwise, saying what it did ("1 step closed and the plan shipped (5 of 5)"). Its second sentence counts the day's sessions, where they were, and how many things they worked on. Then Sessions started this day (N), and under peer_auth a line naming the locked projects this browser has not unlocked, whose work the page leaves out.

Four tiles. Agent time, model tokens, tasks closed (closed as done and still done at the day's end) and kept (the distinct memories, notes and trials written, new or updated). Each states the usual day and draws a trend line over the last active days, then this one; past days also carry the change against the usual day, in percent and never judged good or bad. The usual day is the median of the active days before this one (a day with a session, a task closed or an item kept): up to the 14 most recent within 90 days, and no comparison at all with fewer than 3. Today's tiles show no change, since part of a day against a whole one would read as a fall every morning, and its agent time and tokens say "so far". Each tile jumps to the part of the entry that lists what it counts.

Day rhythm. One column per hour, agent time stacked by agent, the busiest hour's figure on its column. A column's full height stands for at least an hour of agent time, so a light day looks light.

What was worked on. The day is written in threads. A plan thread is one plan in one project: the steps that moved that day and the sessions that moved them or captured, presented or approved the plan. A project thread is one project's tasks outside any plan that moved, and its sessions whose work named no plan or task; sessions in no project make a thread named after their working directory's last folder. The spotlight's threads are cards: the plan's progress before and after the day ("12 → 14 of 14 steps closed"), each task that moved with its status before and after, each session with its agent, what it was about, its agent time and tokens, then the hours it was worked in, the thread's figures, what its sessions kept and the commits it recorded, and a Why this is here disclosure listing the facts that scored. The other threads are one line each under Also that day, and the short sessions one collapsed row, N short sessions.

What a session was about is the first of these that exists: the first line of the findings its agent wrote, its first prompt of the day, the first line of the findings the hooks harvested from its transcript, or "Session in project". The sentence links to the session.

The usage panel. Agents: a ring of model tokens by agent (one client and one model, named as its pill reads), the day's total in the center and a legend row per agent with its share and figure; a day with one agent draws its legend line and no ring. Token mix: output, fresh input, cache write and cache read, as one bar. Projects: bars by agent time, or by model tokens on a day with none. Then Tasks closed, Kept (a superseded or archived memory is marked), and Moments: plans shipped, commits recorded (with what recorded them), flags set, and mishaps the agents reported. Show as table lists every figure the charts draw.

The rail. The month as a heat grid shaded by agent time, then its days, newest first: each with a bar of its agent time against the month's busiest day, the figure, a dot for each of its top projects, and its sessions and character in the tooltip. A run of quiet days is one thin row, and a day from before the usage ledger shows its agent time as "—", not 0m.

The spotlight

A thread scores its outcomes and its effort, each fact capped so that no single one carries a thread alone:

Fact Points At most
The plan shipped: its last open step closed as done 10 10
Each task or step closed as done 3 12
Each task or step created or claimed 1 3
Each memory, note or trial its sessions wrote 1 4
Each commit its tasks or sessions recorded 1 4
Each session that ended with findings its agent wrote 1 2
Agent time 1 for every 10 minutes 12
Output tokens 1 for every 80,000 6

A thread needs 4 points to be a card, and at most six are, most points first. A thread holding a flagged session is always a card, whatever it scored, and counts toward the six. Why this is here lists each fact with the points it scored.

A session's part of a day is short when it has no outcome, under 10 minutes of agent time and under 30,000 output tokens, and is not flagged. An outcome is something the record keeps: a task moved, a plan captured, presented or approved, a memory, note or trial written, a mishap reported, a commit recorded, or an end that day with findings its agent wrote (a summary the hooks harvested does not count). A short session is never a card or part of a thread: it is one line in the folded row, and the character's session and project counts leave it out.

Agent time and model tokens

Agent time is a count of minutes in which an agent sent at least one model message, counted for each session, model and thread (the agent's own turns, and the subagents it launched apart), and added up. Agents working in parallel, and a session beside its subagents, make more agent time than the clock passed.

Model tokens are the four kinds the token mix shows, added: output, fresh input, cache writes and cache reads. They include cache reads, so they are not a billing figure, and the Diary shows no cost.

A day's totals come from the usage ledger with each session counted once; they are never the sum of the cards. Three words mark where a figure is less than whole:

  • Unreported - a session with no token record at all. It is named in a note under the tiles, counted as "(N unreported)" on the tokens tile and on its thread's card, and never counted as zero. A Claude Code session reports at its end, and while the Diary is on its prompts keep it current (mid-session usage); a Codex session reports at each turn's Stop.
  • Approximate - a session from before the usage ledger, which has token totals and no ledger rows. Its whole total counts on the day it ended and on no other ("counted on Nov 12"), with no hour, thread or agent time: the tokens tile says approximate, a note under the tiles says why, and agent time reads "not recorded before the usage ledger". seam usage backfill replaces it with real rows while the session's Claude Code transcript is still on its computer (the command).
  • Shared - a session that worked on more than one thing (two plans, or a plan and loose tasks) is in each thread, and counts in full in each: a card's figures say how many of its sessions are shared, and the cards never add up to the day.

Links

Every link is built from an id resolved, as the page renders, through what this browser may read. An item that no longer exists is plain text titled "No longer exists": the Diary never offers a link that answers 404. A link into an optional feature exists only while that feature is on. A link to an entity opens it beside the day as a peek; a modified click opens the full page.

On the Diary Opens
A day in the rail, a cell of the month grid, the previous or next day, Today That day, in place. A day still to come is never a link; the month arrows keep the day and change the month the rail shows.
A task The task's page.
A session's line, its flag badge The session's page, where its flag and any kept transcript are.
A memory The memory's page; a superseded or archived memory keeps its page, and the Kept list marks it.
A note The note's page.
A trial The trial's page, only while Research is on. With Research off, trials are not on the page at all.
A mishap Its event's page.
A plan: a card's title, a shipped moment The plan's page when it has one in that project; otherwise that project's Plans & tasks tab, as a page; a plan in the global scope with no page is text.
A project chip, a project bar The project's page; the global scope and a working directory are text.
A commit The page of the task or session that recorded it (a commit has no page of its own), with a button to copy its full id.
Sessions started this day (N) The Sessions screen's list for that day, which lists the sessions created on it: hence "started", and N is that list's count. The day's own session count, in the headline, also holds sessions started earlier that worked on it.
A tile The part of this entry that lists what it counts.

The agents legend, the rhythm's columns and the token mix are not links: no page lists "this agent's sessions that day", so they answer on hover only. The other way in is the Sessions screen: a day view there carries Open in Diary while the Diary is on.

Moving around

Keys Does
← / → The previous / next day (today has no next)
t Today
Arrows, Home, End, Esc in a chart Walk its marks, jump to the first or last, rest
Arrows, Enter in the month grid Move a day or a week, open the day

The day keys stand down while you type, while a dialog is open, inside a chart or a peek, and after g, which belongs to the section shortcuts.

How the charts answer. Every mark answers on hover or a tap: a ring segment, an hour of the day rhythm, a project bar, a part of the token mix, a day of the month, a stretch of a card's presence strip. The readout gives its figures and the rest of the chart goes quiet. From the keyboard each chart is one tab stop. Days and project names are real links, so a modified click opens a new tab and the grid works without scripts. Colors name agents only: an agent keeps one color for the whole month, and agents past the month's five busiest share a neutral Other, whose readout names them. A card's presence strip lights whole hours, so its readout gives a stretch of hours, not agent minutes.

Peeks. A peek opens beside the day on a window 1380px wide or more, and under it below that, and the item you clicked stays where it was. Back closes it, and a #peek= link opens the day with it open. Changing the day happens in place and keeps the browser's history.

Today is live. It refreshes in place from the console's live stream, at most every 15 seconds, and an open peek stays open. A past day does not refresh.

On a phone the entry comes first and the month after it, and the tiles go two by two.

With Research off, trials appear nowhere: the day's kept counts, a thread's kept list and its points, the headline and the character are composed without them. The rail and the usual day still count trials among the items kept (counts, never an item).

Empty days

  • A quiet day: "A quiet day.", with no tiles or charts: no session, task or item was recorded.
  • The first run: a day with nothing recorded on it, in its month or in the 90 days before it says "This is the Diary's first page." and draws no stamp.
  • A day still to come: "This day has not begun." and "Still to come.", with Back to today.
  • A day of only short sessions: "Only short sessions: they are folded below."
  • A day from before the usage ledger: totals marked approximate, and agent time not recorded.

The JSON answer

?format=json answers with the day model, the same at every level: the day and its bounds (day, start, end, hours, today), headline, character (word and rule), facts (the tiles' and the character's counts), usage (by agent, project and hour, with the token mix, unreported and approximate), spotlight and also (the threads, each with its score and reasons), short, kept, moments, sessionsStarted and projects; then month (the rail's month, its days and its agents) and usual (the usual day). Every item the day names carries its kind, id, title, resolved and href, the link the page shows, empty when the item no longer resolves or its feature is off. A day still to come answers "future": true with every list empty.

Projects

/console/projects

The board leads with work. Its summary tiles count the agents live (with every model token its projects' sessions used, all time), the open tasks (in progress, ready, blocked, waiting on people, any lapsed or unclaimed claims, and those in locked projects, so the parts add up to the total), the plans moving (a plan with a step still open that moved in the last 7 days, out of every plan with a step open, the rest stalled), then the knowledge base and its reach, judged against its 55% target over the Reach window the header picks (?w=). A locked project's memories count in the knowledge base, which says how many, but not in the reach, which reads only what is outside locked projects.

Each project is one compact row: its name, with its star and badges (isolation, a lock, live agents, and what needs attention), a work line in the task words - "2 plans moving · 1 plan stalled · 1 in progress · 3 ready · 1 blocked · 2 waiting on people" - then its open tasks, its last activity (the later of its last session update and its last task change; hover it for the moment in your own time) and its reach as a small figure. The whole row opens the project. Blocked and waiting on people count exactly what the Tasks page's JSON rails and counts count with its plan steps shown (?steps=1): blocked waits on unfinished work alone, and waiting on people is a gate or a step an open gate holds.

Needs attention means something waits on you or is stuck: a lapsed claim, a task marked in progress that no claim holds, an open gate, a captured plan awaiting approval, or data under a slug the project registry does not list. A project whose tasks only wait on other work is not flagged, and neither is a retired one. The header's chip counts them, and choosing it narrows the board to them (?show=attention; all, the default, shows every project); narrowed, the chip's Show all clears it.

The board has three views (?group=activity|family|flat):

  • Activity, the default: Active (a live agent, or a session or task touched in the last 30 days), then Quiet, then Retired. Quiet and Retired are folded. A filter (?q=) that matches a project inside one opens it, and Quiet stands open when no project is Active.
  • Family: each shared-briefing family, a parent with its children under it, then Standalone, then Retired by split, folded.
  • Flat: every project in one list.

?sort=recent|coverage|name|favorites orders the rows inside each band. In the Activity view, Recent puts starred projects first, then those with a live agent, then the most recent.

The global ("") scope is not a project, so no view lists it. It is one line under the summary tiles, "Shared context: N memories, N notes, reach N%", linking to Context.

Under peer_auth, a locked project this browser has not unlocked is a row in the same bands, sorted with the others, with a lock badge: its name, its counts, its last activity (the latest session start or end in it, never a title) and Unlock, which opens /console/unlock/<project>. Nothing else about it is read: it has no work line, and it is never judged to need attention, so the attention view leaves it out. A task that waits on a locked project's task counts as blocked, as it does on the Tasks page. The JSON model also lists these tallies as locked.

The board remembers the view and sort you pick, in this browser only (its local storage). A link that names neither, such as the sidebar's, shows the remembered pair, drawn in place without a reload; a URL that names a view or a sort wins. A fresh browser starts on Activity, sorted by Recent.

Selecting a project opens the project workspace - a seven-tab page over that project alone. It opens on Plans & tasks (?tab=tasks), and a load reads and renders only the tab it shows: the header and the tab counts come from the project's board row. A tab is a ?tab= link that loads in place, so switching keeps the page, back and forward walk the tabs, and a live refresh redraws only the tab on screen. ?tab= takes tasks, overview, sessions, memories, notes, interactions and context; ?tab=plans and the Context tab's old name, ?tab=relations, redirect to their tab. ?from=<project> with no tab opens Memories, and ?isolate=<state> with no tab opens Overview. The Interactions and Context tabs are those screens over one project, so they follow their level: below Advanced they leave the tab bar, and a ?tab= link still opens them, under the level note.

Tab Shows
Plans & tasks One card per plan. Its head is titled by the plan's narrative note (by its slug when it has none), with plan:<slug> beside it to copy, the status in words (draft, awaiting approval, approved), a narrative link to the note, and a line that counts the steps by their status words ("2/6 done · 1 in progress · 1 blocked · 2 waiting on owner"). stalled 10d marks a plan with open steps, none in progress, that nothing moved for 7 days, with "ready work, nobody on it" when a step is claimable. A captured plan that is a draft or awaits approval, or is approved with no steps yet, is a card too, with no steps; Approve, on a capture that awaits it, lands back on its card. Then each plan's step timeline: each step's word, claiming session, lease countdown, and blocking dependency. A step a gate holds is waiting: it says who must act and what must happen ("waits on owner: approve the window") and is never claimable, and a gate's row is marked Gate and says what it holds ("holds 2 steps"). The completed plans fold below the cards; past the first 20, N older opens Plans for the project. Then Off-plan tasks: every task of the project outside a plan, once, grouped In progress (holder and lease), Ready, Blocked (the first blocker named and linked), Waiting on people (who must act, and what must happen), Gates (what each one holds: the unfinished tasks that depend on it) and, folded, the ten most recently closed, whose all closed opens the Tasks screen on the project's closed tasks. Its line ("8 open: 5 in plans, 3 off-plan") counts what the tab lists, the number on the tab's pill. Every row, a step or an off-plan task, expands into the task's dossier in place and copies its task's whole id, and each plan's head copies plan:<slug>. A task in progress that no live claim holds carries a strip under its row: claim lapsed offers release claim, which lands back on the row, unclaimed (marked in progress with no claim at all) opens the task under its row.
Overview The project's metrics, memory kinds, injection trend, its Isolation card, and its own recent events.
Sessions The project's sessions counted by state (live, idle, completed, expired), the newest 60 of them, and a link to all of them on the Sessions screen. Each row is titled as the Sessions screen titles it (the task a live session holds, else its first prompt), with its name under it, and a live session names each task it holds by title, linked to the task.
Memories The project's memories with a lineage cell - provenance session, or a supersession pointer - plus the memories it inherits from a parent that a strict per-slug count excludes.
Notes The project's notes.
Interactions The project-scoped slice of the feed.
Context The effective SessionStart flow into and out of the project: global and parent memory pools, sibling-family channels, and split lineage.

Came from. With access requests on, an item written by an agent that held a confidential or sealed project's content carries a provenance stamp ("may contain content from example-finance (grant R-7F3K)"). On a project with such items, the Memories, Notes and Plans & tasks tabs show the stamp on each row and a Came from bar: one chip per project the stamps name, with how many items of that tab's kind name it. Choosing one (?from=<project>) narrows the three tabs to those items, and Plans & tasks then lists the tasks themselves, any status. A locked project this browser has not unlocked is named only; the items listed are this project's own. A project with no stamped item shows no bar.

Locks. Under peer_auth, a confidential or sealed project's Isolation card offers Lock this project, which opens /console/lock/<project>. Locking it, and removing a lock set here, each need a passkey already enrolled on the Approvers page; without one the card links there. Seamless restarts to apply the change. A project listed under peer_auth.force_locked shows as Force locked and cannot be changed here. A locked project's isolation cannot be set to open.

The lock page, /console/lock/<project>, is one card. Its title asks the change it offers ("Lock example-conf?", or "Remove the lock on example-conf?" for a lock set here), and a ladder of Open, the project's fence (Confidential, or Sealed) and Locked marks where the project stands and where the change takes it. Two rows say what the change does to the project's own agents and to this console, then one passkey button (in the danger tone to remove a lock), with a chip saying Seamless restarts to apply it. After the passkey the card shows the change's steps, approved, restarting and done, and the page then refreshes in place. An open project's card links to its Isolation card instead, and with no passkey enrolled it links to the Approvers page. A force lock names peer_auth.force_locked, with a copy button and a link to unlock the project in this browser instead. A change saved but not applied yet says it takes effect when Seamless next restarts. The JSON model adds isolation, rung (open, confidential, sealed or locked) and rung_to.

The unlock page, /console/unlock/<project>, is the same card for a locked project: a lock, the project's name, a Locked chip beside the lock's kind (config file, from the console with a link to remove it, or lock removed while a removed lock waits for the next restart), and its counts as tiles. With a passkey enrolled, its one primary action is Unlock for 3 hours (the console's lease, shorter when peer_auth.max_lease is), and Approve from a terminal waits under "no passkey here?". With no passkey enrolled, passkeys off, or this browser on another address than the passkey's, Approve from a terminal is the primary action, with a line saying why. It turns the card into numbered steps: this browser's code, large, with its time left, then the command with a copy button, and Cancel. Once the command approves the code, the card turns unlocked in place, without a reload. Unlocked here, the lock opens, the chip reads Unlocked here, the time left shows as a bar and in words, and Open leads (the project, or the plan, session or conversation a locked page sent you from), with Lock it again now under it. A caller that is not a browser is told an unlock is per browser. The JSON model adds lock_kind: file, console, or empty for a removed lock the next restart applies.

A retired project still renders, with its banner - kept for provenance. Only an unknown slug is a 404. An error page under /console/projects/<slug> (a mistyped tab, say) offers Back to when that project exists.

Sessions

/console/sessions, /console/sessions/{id}, /console/sessions/{id}/transcript

The list separates active (live: active and heartbeated within the idle TTL) from idle (active but gone quiet past it, awaiting the reaper) from completed and expired. Filterable by status, searchable, windowed, and filterable by retention (?retained=yes|no): whether the session left a durable artifact behind - non-empty findings, or a written memory, note, or recorded trial, the same covered-ness test the coverage numbers apply. The Overview's continuity vital links straight to ?retained=no, so its click answers "which sessions dropped knowledge".

A row is titled by what the session is doing: the task it holds with a live claim (and how many more it holds), else its first prompt, chosen and shortened as the Diary's about line is. Findings its agent wrote come first, so a session that has them keeps its name as the title and shows them. A titled row's second line is the session's generated name (cc/...).

?project=<slug> lists one project's sessions (global lists the global scope's), over all time unless a window is chosen, and every filter and sort link keeps it. A value that names no project this console reads is refused like any other bad value; a locked project's refusal says it is locked, and its sessions stay out.

The list defaults to the last 24 hours (?w=24h|7d|30d|all; any other value is refused). When that leaves most sessions out, the list ends by saying so ("3 of 212 sessions were active in the last 24h") and offers the wider windows in place, so a quiet day never reads as an empty system. The list shows the newest 200 sessions its filters keep, and past that says so ("Newest 200 of 559"). The search and every filter apply before that cap, so a session older than the newest 200 is still found; each word searched for must appear in the session's name, project, findings or id. A row names its host only when the session ran on a different machine from the console's, and its source only when it was not a normal startup.

A day view (?day=YYYY-MM-DD, what a click on the momentum calendar opens) lists the sessions started on that day, whatever the window. While the Diary is on, its heading carries Open in Diary, that day's page.

A session's page is the workspace: its findings (rendered), its event timeline as interaction rows, per-session counts over the events the timeline holds (tool calls, memory reads and writes, items injected, and read-after-inject), the tasks it currently claims with their lease countdowns, and what it did: Tasks moved (each task it created, claimed, released, closed or reopened, with those moves in order), the notes it wrote, and the memories it produced. Only items this console still reads are listed, each linking to its page. With none, the card says what fits the session: an active one has nothing durable yet, a finished one moved no task and wrote nothing. The timeline holds 500 events; a longer session's says "The first 500 of N events" and links to the latest 500 (?timeline=latest, which links back; any other value is refused). The page's title, the browser tab's, is the session's name and project.

A flagged session carries a badge with its verdict (good, bad or notable) and its reason on the list, the peek and its page. Its page adds a card: when it was flagged, the transcript file the agent client wrote, and what became of the copy, with Download JSONL while a copy is kept (/console/sessions/{id}/transcript, the owner's alone: never a restricted account, a relay's caller or a paired device). Once any session is flagged, the list offers a Flag filter (?verdict=flagged|good|bad|notable). With no window chosen it lists the flagged sessions of all time, as seam sessions --flagged does: a flag changes no session's last update, so the 24-hour default would hide a session flagged after its day. A window chosen under Updated applies to the filter as to every other, and stays chosen while the other filters change; until then the page's links carry none.

The conversation

With access requests on, a conversation can span sessions: a move into a fenced project continues it as a child session there. Every session of a conversation that moved, asked for or holds a grant, or wrote a stamped item shows one Conversation card (also in the page's JSON as conversation):

  • Home chain: the session it started in and each move's child, oldest first, with the move's request, who decided it and when.
  • Reach: every project it reached - its homes, projects session_start bound it to, read-only and read-and-write grants, leases, and requests still waiting, denied or expired - each with its request (R-...) and who decided it: a passkey or Touch ID key by name, the terminal (seamlessd approve), the bearer key (seam approve or the console, advisory), the agent's approval dialog (advisory), or a Deny on this console.
  • Written: what its sessions wrote, by project, each with its provenance stamp.

A locked project this browser has not unlocked shows its name, the request that reached it and an Unlock link back to the page, and nothing from inside. A conversation that never moved, asked for nothing and wrote nothing stamped shows no card.

Mishaps

/console/mishaps

Every mishap agents reported at session_end, newest first, for a recurrence review: which kinds keep happening, and which memories fail to prevent them. Its sidebar row is under Live, at every level, with a count of the reports since you last marked them reviewed (nothing at zero), and g then f opens it; the Overview's mishap card and the check-in's mishap count open it too.

  • Type chips - All, then each type with its count - shell-trap, wrong-target, live-state, ignored-warning, fabricated, other - and untyped: reports that named no type, among them every report written before types existed. The counts cover the project and window in view whatever type is selected; point at a chip for what its type means.
  • Your review - how many reports arrived since you last marked them reviewed, whatever the filters, with Mark reviewed, and a new mark on each of those reports. Marking them reviewed clears the Overview's mishap card until another report arrives; it marks through the newest report the page drew, so one that arrives while you read stays new.
  • Reports - each with its type (or untyped), its text with the type prefix taken off, its project (click it to keep only that scope's reports), the session that reported it with its agent, and the memories it named. Click a row to read its event in the reading panel.
  • Memories named - every memory the reports in view named, with how many named it. A memory many reports name is one that is not preventing its mishap.

Filters: ?type= (a type, or untyped), ?project= (a slug, or global), and the window ?w=24h|7d|30d|all (all time by default) or ?days=N. A value the page cannot read is a 400 naming what it takes. ?format=json answers total, types (each with its count and meaning), shown (the reports the filters select), mishaps (each with type, text, the recorded description, project, sessionId, session and memories), memories (each with its count), review (at, when you last marked the reports reviewed, and new, how many arrived since; absent while no report exists), each report's new, and locked while peer_auth leaves locked projects out. The list holds the newest 200.

An item's own page

/console/memories/{id}, /console/notes/{id}, /console/tasks/{id}, /console/plans/{slug}?project=<slug>

A link to one memory, note, task or plan opens that item on a page of its own: the item and what is around it, never the list it lives in. The lists stay on Memories, Notes, Tasks and Plans. Every item reads the same way:

  • The way back, top left: a link to the collection scoped to the item's project ("example-ops's memories"), or to the list the URL names. The browser's Back button works as always.
  • Its place, top right: "3 of 12 gotchas in example-ops", with previous and next (k and j). When the URL carries a list's state (the parameters the list puts on its links: ?sort=, ?kind=, ?project=, ?q= and the rest), the place follows that list's order. Without one it is the memory's project and kind, newest first; the note's project, newest first (an agent's working copy among them with the working copies shown); a plan step's plan, its closed steps in the order they closed and then the rest as the plan card orders them; or an off-plan task's project, as the Tasks list orders it. A list that does not hold the item falls back to that. A row of the Memories or the Notes list always carries its list's state (?sort=recent on the default list), so a memory or a note opened from it is placed in that list.
  • Where it lives: project › Memories › kind, project › Notes, project › Plans › plan:<slug>, or project › Tasks, each a link.
  • The title row: a memory's name in mono, or a note's or a task's title, with copy and the star, and the actions where the eye starts: Edit in editor and Archive for a memory, Edit in editor and Delete for a note, and for a task the actions its reader offers (Mark done, Waits on someone, Drop, Reopen, Release claim). Every action returns to this page with the list's state kept. A deleted note has no page left, so Delete returns to the way back.
  • The lead and the facts: the description, then one line of facts. A task's line starts with its whole id and Copy id, the form you hand an agent.
  • The body in one reading column, and a context column beside it, which moves under the body on a narrow screen:
    • a memory: In use (how often it surfaced, how long ago, its utility score, the sessions it surfaced to), what replaced it and what it replaces, up to five more of its kind in its project with a link to all, and its file path;
    • a note: On this page (its h2 and h3 headings as links, once there are two), the plans it is part of with their progress, more notes in its project (its working copies left out, as on the list), and its file path;
    • a task: its plan as a small card with every step and this one marked, what it depends on and what it blocks. Its history and earlier versions follow the body;
    • a plan (/console/plans/{slug}?project=<slug>, drawn by Plans): its narrative note, the notes attached to it and its project. A plan has no place in a list, so its page has no previous or next.

An archived or superseded memory keeps its banner and Restore at the top of the page, and a note Held keeps says so there. A locked project's item answers as it always did, and its items are absent from every other item's place. ?format=json, ?peek=1 and ?reader=1 answer as before.

Memories

/console/memories, /console/memories/{id}

One list, full width, with no rail and no reader: a memory's link opens its own page. With All projects in scope the list is every match, newest first, in local-day groups: Today, Yesterday, Earlier this week (the seven days up to today), Earlier this month and Older, each heading saying how many matches it holds. Days are counted in the daemon's time zone, as the Diary counts them. The list draws 50 rows at a time, and Show 50 more adds the next rows in place, without reloading the page; the address keeps how many are shown (?show=). The other sorts, Name, Reach (how often a memory surfaced), Utility and Starred, draw the matches as one group in that order, 50 at a time. With a project chosen in the switcher, the list is the whole project, grouped by kind in the canonical order, each kind's heading with the one line that says what that kind holds, and each kind in the sort's order.

A row is one link: the kind as a colored word, the name in mono, the description on one line, the project (on the All projects list only), how long since it changed, and, from the Standard level, "surfaced 43×" or "never surfaced". A memory written by a restricted local account says so on its row.

The bar holds the project switcher, the text filter (/ focuses it), Starred, Never surfaced (memories that have never reached an agent's context, from the Standard level), Sort, and N archived and superseded. Under it the kind chips filter by kind: All kinds, then each kind with a match. The filters combine, and every chip, toggle and switcher row counts what choosing it would show, the other filters applied. The text box matches a substring of the name, the description, the kind, a tag, or the project's slug or name. While anything is filtered the header reads "3 of 128 active" beside a Clear link; when nothing matches, the list says so and offers Clear and Search everything for the same text on Search.

N archived and superseded switches the list to the memories that were archived or replaced (?status=inactive), laid out the same way: each row says which it is and, when superseded, names the memory that replaced it. Every filter, the switcher and the sort keep it, and pressed again it brings back the active memories. Its Search everything reaches the archived memories too.

The project is chosen with the switcher, the In All projects button (p opens it). It lists All projects; Recent, the projects this browser last chose or visited (up to five, kept in this browser only); Starred projects; then every project that holds a match, most active first by its latest session or task, as on Projects, and Shared globally last. Each row counts what choosing it would show, the other filters applied. Projects with no activity in 30 days fold into one line that says how many there are, and typing finds them. Typing filters by slug or display name in the page, with no request; the arrow keys move, Enter chooses, Esc closes, and Backspace in an empty field goes back to All projects. A locked project this browser has not unlocked is listed with a lock and no count, and links to its unlock page. Without script the switcher is a plain menu of the same links.

The whole state is in the URL: ?sort=, ?kind=, ?project= (a slug, or global), ?fav=1, ?surfaced=never, ?q=, ?status=inactive and ?show=. A value the screen cannot read is a 400 naming the values it takes. ?group=project, from the list before, is still read and kept on links, and changes nothing: choosing a project replaces it. Each row's link carries the list's state (?sort=recent on the default list), so the memory's page places it in this list and its k / j walk it; a new filter, sort or project starts again at the first 50 rows. Starring, archiving and restoring on the memory's page return to that page with the list's state kept. ?format=json answers every match, unpaged, in project and kind groups with the archived and superseded ones beside them, whatever the page draws.

What reaches an agent's context is surfaced here, the word the Overview and the knowledge sky use: a row reads "surfaced 43×" or "never surfaced", and a memory's page leads with how long since it last surfaced, or says it never has. A kind's tooltip, on a row or a chip, is the same one-line meaning its group heading shows in a project's list.

A memory's own page renders the body uncapped (through the markdown layer, with raw HTML disabled and a sanitizer on the output), the metadata (kind, project, tags, timestamps, the session that produced it), how often it surfaced and was read, the sessions it surfaced to, its utility score with the per-signal demand breakdown behind it, the vscode:// link straight to the file, and its supersession neighbors in both directions: what replaced it, and what it replaced. Its actions are the star, the flag that pins it into briefings and boosts recall, and archive, which asks in the page first and says what happens: the memory leaves briefings and recall, its history stays readable, and it can be restored. An archived or superseded memory says so in a banner at the top of the page, and the banner carries Restore, unless a memory that replaced it is still active, which the banner links instead, or Held holds it, which the banner says.

j and k move a focus ring through the rows, Enter opens the focused memory's page, / focuses the filter and p opens the switcher. A memory written while the page is open joins its group as the page refreshes in place, without a reload, and the row in focus keeps the ring.

Notes

/console/notes, /console/notes/{id}

One list, full width, in the Memories list's shape, with no rail and no reader: a note's link opens its own page. The list is every match, newest first, in local-day groups (Today, Yesterday, Earlier this week, Earlier this month and Older), each heading saying how many matches it holds, across every project or, with a project chosen in the switcher, in that one. It draws 50 rows at a time; Show 50 more, or Show the other N when fewer are left, adds the next rows in place, and the address keeps how many are shown (?show=). Name (A to Z) and Starred draw the matches as one group in that order.

A row is one link: the title, the description on one line, each plan the note belongs to (its plan:<slug> tags) with the plan's status (a captured plan's own, otherwise in progress, ready or done from its steps), up to two of its tags and how many more, the project (on the All projects list only), its length in words and how long since it changed. A note written by a restricted local account says so on its row.

The bar holds the project switcher (the same one as on Memories, where the global scope reads Global inbox), the text filter (/ focuses it; a substring of the title, the description, a tag, or the project's slug or name), Starred and Sort. Under it the tag chips filter by tag: Everything, plan narratives (the notes tagged plan:<slug>), then the tags written for people that most notes in view carry, up to twelve; any other tag is found by typing it. The tags software adds - created-by:*, plan-status:*, cc-plan and agent-cache - never become chips. Every chip, toggle and switcher row counts what choosing it would show, the other filters applied, and the "N of M" header, Clear and the Search fallback work as on Memories.

Planning subagents' cached runs (the notes tagged agent-cache, agents' working copies) are folded away by default: they are left out of the list and its counts, and a line after the chips says "N agent working copies folded · show them". show them (?caches=1) lists them among the notes, each marked as a working copy, and every chip, filter, sort and the switcher keep that; fold them folds them again. A plan's page and its card on Plans still list them under their plan.

The whole state is in the URL: ?sort=, ?project= (a slug, or global), ?fav=1, ?q=, ?tag=, ?plans=1, ?caches=1 and ?show=. A value the screen cannot read is a 400 naming the values it takes. ?group=project, from the rail before, is still read and kept on links, and changes nothing. Each row's link carries the list's state (?sort=recent on the default list), so the note's page places it in this list and its k / j walk it. ?format=json answers every match of the filters, unpaged, in project groups (global first), the working copies included, whatever the page draws.

A note's own page renders it as a document: its plans with their status, its tags (the ones software adds fold behind a +N chip), its length and reading time, its source URL, and the file path with an editor link. Its actions are the star and Delete. Delete asks in the page first and removes the note for good. A note that is a plan's narrative says so, and also needs the box beside Delete ticked; while Held holds the note, the page says why instead.

j and k move a focus ring through the rows, Enter opens the focused note's page, / focuses the filter and p opens the switcher.

Tasks

/console/tasks, /console/tasks/{id}

The backlog, as one list, full width, with no rail and no reader. By default it lists every project's tasks outside a plan, which is what tasks_ready means for an agent; Plan steps too adds the plan steps, each with its plan:<slug> chip, and the header's count follows it. The list draws its groups in this order, each heading saying how many it holds, and the pills under the bar jump to them:

  • Needs you: a gate waiting on you, a claim whose lease lapsed, and a task marked in progress that no claim holds, the tasks the Overview's Needs you cards and the sidebar's Tasks badge count. A plan step that waits on you is here whatever Plan steps too says.
  • In progress: held by a live claim.
  • Ready: the first 10 in the sort's order, then "N more ready - show them", which draws every one (?ready=all).
  • Blocked: waiting on unfinished work, a step that only your own gates hold among them.
  • Waiting on others: the gates on anyone else, then the steps such a gate holds, or whose own gate waits on someone else.
  • Recently closed: done and dropped in the last 7 days, newest first (the newest 25 of them), folded; All N closed tasks pages through every closed task.

A row is the task's state mark and title, with one line that says what holds it: a gate's who and what, and how many tasks it holds; when a claim lapsed and whose it was; a live claim's holder, its lease and when it started; how long a task has been ready, or untouched once nothing changed on it for 30 days; its first blocker, linked, and how many more; who it waits on; when it closed. Then the last 8 characters of its id, which copy the whole id, its project, its plan, and the one action the row needs: Mark as handled on a gate waiting on you, Release claim on a lapsed claim (it asks in the page first), and Mark done on a ready task or one in progress that no live claim holds. A row a live claim holds offers no action. Each posts to the route the task's own page posts to, and lands back on the list at the row, wherever its new group puts it, with the filters kept and a line that says what it did. The title, or a click on the row, opens the task in the reading panel; j and k move a focus ring through the titles, Enter opens the focused task's own page, / focuses the filter and p opens the switcher.

The URL holds the filters, so a link keeps them: ?project=<slug> (global for the global scope; the project switcher, the same one as on Memories, lists the projects with open tasks and their counts), ?plan=<slug> (one plan's steps; plan:<slug> works too), ?q=<text> (title, body or id; a pasted short id finds its task), ?steps=1 (plan steps too), ?ready=all (every ready task), ?closed=all (every closed task, 25 to a page, with &page=N) and ?sort=oldest|newest (oldest first, the order agents claim in, is the default). A value the page cannot read, or a project or plan it holds no task of (a locked one's included), is a 400 that names what it takes. The JSON model (?format=json) carries the rails as before (ready, inProgress, blocked, gates, gated, and closed, a page of the newest closed tasks) with projects, filter and counts, which count as the project board does: in progress is a live claim's alone, lapsed claims and unclaimed starts are counted apart, and waiting on people is the gates and the steps they hold together. counts.open, the head's N open, is every unfinished row the list draws, so it also counts the plan steps that wait on you, which Needs you draws while plan steps are toggled off. It adds the list's needsYou (the Needs you group, in its order) and closedRecent (how many tasks closed in the last 7 days).

A task's own page and the panel carry the task's body, claim and lease state, both dependency directions, its History, and the owner's actions on the task, the same as the peek (the step dossier on a project's Plans & tasks tab): Mark done and Drop on an open or in-progress task (a gate whose gate is still open closes by Mark as handled instead of Mark done), Reopen on a closed one, Mark as handled with a note on an open gate, Waits on someone on an open or in-progress task whose own gate is not open (who must act and what must happen, the decision and when it is ready optional: the task leaves the ready queue for the people's until its gate is marked as handled), and Release claim on a task in progress, whoever holds it or none. Drop and Release claim ask in the page: the button turns into a second one to press. While a live claim holds the task the page names its holder and offers Release claim first: the console never closes a task over its holder's head. Each action returns to the page it came from, its filters kept, with a line that says what it did. A task's own URL opens its own page.

The history lists what happened to the task, oldest first, from its task.transition events: created, claimed, released, reopened, done or dropped, its gate set and cleared, each with the session that did it (linked when the console can read it, you for an action from this console) and when. A holder's renewed claim reads once, with how many times.

Every task and plan step says where it stands in the same words, on Tasks, the project workspace and Plans:

Word Means
ready Open, with nothing unfinished before it: an agent can claim it now.
in progress Held by a live claim.
blocked Open, waiting on unfinished work before it.
waiting on who A gate, or a step an open gate holds - its own, or a gate it depends on - named by who must act (waiting on owner).
claim lapsed In progress, but its holder's lease ran out: any agent can claim it.
unclaimed Marked in progress without a claim (seam task start, or tasks_update status=in_progress): any agent can claim it.
done, dropped Closed.

A task's holder and creator are named by their session and link to its page when the console can read it. The lease reads lease live, 12m left while the claim holds and lapsed 3m ago once it runs out.

Each task row - a row of the Tasks list, a plan step, an off-plan row, a dependency - shows the last 8 characters of the task's id and copies the whole id, the form you hand an agent (run <id>): on the Tasks list the short id is the copy button itself; elsewhere a copy button beside it stays quiet until you hover or focus the row, and on a touch screen it is always there. A plan copies as plan:<slug>.

Hover a relative time (3d) to see the moment it names, in your browser's own time; without JavaScript the hover shows it in UTC.

Under a lock, a task blocked by a task in a locked project you haven't unlocked sits in the blocked rail, its blocker named only by project on a line of its own; the task's reader and peek list it under Depends on the same way. The project workspace's Plans & tasks tab marks such steps blocked, and lists such an off-plan task under Blocked, never as ready. Opening a plan or a session that lives in a locked project takes you to that project's unlock page, which says the item is there and links back once you unlock it.

Locks

/console/locks, /console/locks/{id}

Only while the Repo locks optional feature is on; a Standard screen. Every repo lock, shown with its repository and its name (LOCK seamless main): the refs it guards, whether it is free, held (in the accent tone) or lapsed (in the warning tone), the session that holds it with since and until, or when it lapsed, each with its date (and the restricted account that session belongs to, when it is one), the lock's queue while sessions wait for it (how many, and the next one, with its account when it is a restricted account's), the repository identities that resolve to it, and the projects whose restricted accounts may hold it. A lock belongs to no project, so the page lists every one; a holder or a next waiter in a project this browser has not unlocked reads "a session this console does not show", and such a listed project is left out.

  • Waiting for your approval - the declarations restricted accounts filed: nobody can hold one until you Approve it, and Discard leaves the repository free to be declared again. The sidebar badge counts them.
  • Force release - on a held or lapsed lock: ends the hold whoever holds it. The agent that held it is not told, so release a lock only when its holder is gone or stuck. On a live hold it asks in the page first; a lapsed one is released at once.

/console/locks/{id} is the same page with that lock marked; with ?format=json, the lock alone.

Plans

/console/plans, /console/plans/{slug}?project=<slug>

One board of plan cards for every project: the card a project's Plans & tasks tab shows, the same template, grouped by the state the plan is in, top to bottom:

Group What puts a plan there
Needs you A captured plan you can approve (a draft, or presented and awaiting approval), a step waiting on people (an open gate, its own or one it depends on), or a step in progress that no live claim holds (a lapsed claim, or one started with none).
In progress A live claim holds a step.
Stalled Open steps, none in progress, and nothing moved for 7 days.
Ready Everything else still open: open steps that moved in the last 7 days, or a plan with no steps yet.
Shipped Every step closed, done or dropped (a dropped step closes a plan as a done one does), or a captured plan the gardener settled.

Needs you and In progress cards open with their steps; Stalled and Ready cards show their head line ("3/5 done · 1 ready · 1 blocked · moved 9d ago") and load their steps when opened. On the board a step names its nearest blocker; the plan's page names the whole chain. Only Shipped is windowed (24h, 7d, 30d, All time; 24h by default) and folded, with how many shipped before the window and the wider windows: an active plan is never hidden by a window. Every card carries its project as a chip that opens that project's Plans & tasks tab at the plan, and Approve on a card returns to the card on the board, its filters kept.

The project is chosen with the switcher Memories draws, the In All projects button (p opens it): All projects, Recent, Starred, then each project with a plan on the board, most active first, and the global scope, global, last. Each row counts the plans choosing it would show, and keeps the text filter and the window; projects with no activity in 30 days fold away and typing finds them; a locked project this browser has not unlocked is listed with a lock and no count, and links to its unlock page. ?project=<slug> narrows the board to one (global names the global scope); a project that is not there, or that is locked and not unlocked in this browser, is a 400. ?q= keeps the plans whose title or slug holds the text, in any case (plan:<slug> works too). A title holding " -- " shows it as a colon, as every title does (see the top of this page); the stored title is untouched.

A plan is keyed by its project and slug: the same slug in two projects is two plans, with their own steps and notes. /console/plans/{slug}?project=<slug> is one plan's own page, read as a memory, a note or a task is: the way back to the project's plans, project › Plans, then the title row (the narrative note's title with copy and the star; plan:<slug> to copy; the status in words, a capture's own or else the group the board puts the plan in; the stalled mark; and Approve while a capture awaits it, which returns to the page), then one line of facts: where it came from, its steps done of all and the rest counted by their words, its model tokens and when it was updated. The body column is its steps first, in dependency order (a step below the steps it depends on, otherwise in the order they were written), each with its holder, its blockers and the gates it waits on, then its narrative; beside it, the narrative note, the notes attached to it (supporting notes and agent caches) and the project, which opens its Plans & tasks tab at the plan when it has a workspace. A plan whose steps exist with no note tagged plan:<slug> in its project still opens: its page says it has no narrative note yet, and has nothing to star. Every plan link the console renders names its project (the board, the project tab, the plan's page, Overview, Now, the Diary, Search, a task's own page, notes and the Gardener); a slug that is a plan in more than one project, opened without ?project=, answers a chooser naming each project's plan (with ?format=json, a 409 that names them), never one page holding both. A plan's source reads "captured from plan mode" (a Claude Code capture, with its plan file, iteration and agent runs) or "from tasks" (a composed plan). Approve appears for captures only.

With ?format=json the board is rows (each plan the board lists, in its order, with its state and href), the group counts (needsYou, inProgress, stalled, ready, done for the shipped plans the window lists, shippedAll), total, projects (the menu) and filter; a plan's page is its row, body, attached notes and tasks (its steps in the page's order, each with its word, holder and the gates it waits on).

Each plan also carries a model tokens rollup - the cumulative transcript tokens of every session attributed to the plan (any session that moved a step, or captured the plan) - compact on its card (~483k tok) and qualified on its page (~483k model tokens · 3 sessions (1 unreported)). Attribution is whole-session on purpose: tokens are only ever known per session, so a session's full burn counts toward each plan it touched, counted once however many steps it moved. Claude Code reports tokens at session end (and, while the Diary is on, as its prompts keep its usage current), so a live session stays unreported until then; a session that touched more than one plan is disclosed as shared rather than split by guesswork - which is also why plan totals must never be summed across plans.

Labs

/console/labs, /console/labs/{name}

The research-lab surface (the console twin of lab_open / trial_record / trial_query). Labs and Trials are one optional feature and ship off; while it is off both screens answer with a short "switched off" page and neither appears in the nav.

A lab is not a stored entity - it is the label its trials carry, a stable name for one line of investigation - so this screen is an aggregation over the trials table and there is nothing to write.

The same library shape: a rail of labs, most recently active first, each with its trial count and pass/fail tallies. The reader shows one lab's whole identity - outcome tallies (pass, fail, partial, inconclusive, and other for free-form or empty outcomes), the projects and sessions its trials touched, first and last activity - and its trial history, newest first, each entry linking into the Trials screen. Long histories cap at 100 with a pointer to the uncapped, filterable view.

Trials

/console/trials, /console/trials/{id}

The flat, filterable view over every recorded trial - the console twin of the trial_query MCP tool, and part of the same optional feature as Labs. The rail groups trials by lab (a group sits where its newest trial does) and filters by ?lab= and ?outcome=. Choosing an outcome opens the list anew, with its newest match in the reader, never beside the trial that was open. Outcomes are free-form by design, so ?outcome= is an exact-match filter rather than a validated enum; the seg offers the conventional values (pass, fail, partial, inconclusive).

The reader shows one trial's full record: what changed, expected vs actual side by side (the actual pane tinted by outcome), the structured metrics trial_record captured, and its provenance - lab, project, and the recording session, each linked. Trial hits also surface in search and the command palette, and a session's page lists the trials it recorded.

Context

/console/context

The briefing topology that the plans board does not show: which knowledge pools are eligible at SessionStart, which configured edges are currently enabled by the effective briefing settings, and where project splits moved durable memory. It covers global memory, one-way parent-memory inheritance, bidirectional sibling families (findings and the opt-in memory channel), unregistered-project warnings, and retired-project split lineage reconstructed from the memory-move event log.

?scope=all (All projects) renders every known project, with global memory shown as the shared source pool; ?scope=project&project=<slug> focuses the same topology on one project. The legacy /console/relations route permanently redirects here and preserves its query string.

Reachable from the Projects board.

Retrieval

/console/retrieval

The circulation report: is stored knowledge actually reaching agents, and at what cost? The hero pairs the reach ring (distinct active memories that surfaced, over all active memories) with the window's volume and cost - injections, sessions reached, and estimated tokens injected. Everything follows the selectable observation window except where a panel says otherwise.

Five zones below it:

  1. Delivery path - the funnel as a flow: injections → distinct memories → sessions reached, ending in the knowledge-base coverage meter (how many active memories are still waiting to surface).
  2. Circulation pattern - the injection trend chart and the traffic-by-kind mix.
  3. Project coverage - reach per project (the global scope first), each row with its own reach rate and injection count.
  4. Knowledge pressure - the most-injected memories against quiet knowledge: active memories not updated, injected, or read within gardener.staleness_days (90 days by default), the horizon the gardener's staleness pass proposes archives by, and the label says the configured value. Unlike everything else on the page, the stale list is all-time, not windowed. Each row links to its memory and, when the gardener already holds a pending proposal for it (an archive, a merge, a move, a reclassification), to that proposal: proposal waiting. The staleness pass never proposes archiving a constraint, a stage, or a memory another memory links to, so such a row can stand without one.
  5. Loop health - push versus pull: is what briefings push also what agents pull? Demand rate is the share of briefed memories that were also pulled by a query; waste share is the share of injected tokens spent on memories with no query-gated demand, judged against a fixed trailing 30 days whatever the window. Two miss stats sit side by side and measure different paths: the recall-miss rate is ambient - prompts that matched no memory on the <seam-recall> path - while agent search misses are deliberate recall calls that found nothing; recurring ones feed the gardener's memory-wanted pass. Funnel by surface splits the read-after-inject funnel by injection surface - session-start briefings versus subagent-start child injections - each with its injections, distinct memories, and the share pulled by a query-gated read within the following 24 hours. The zone closes with the dead weight panel: memories briefings kept injecting without a single recall hit, prompt match, or read in 30 days (constraints and stages exempt as pinned-by-design) - the evidence behind the gardener's dead-weight archive proposals. Its rows link to a waiting proposal the same way.

Reachable from the Overview's reach, injections and sessions-reached vitals and its going-stale card, at Advanced.

Gardener

/console/gardener

The review queue. Each pending proposal renders as a card showing exactly what it would do - the memory to archive and why (whether staleness, a dead stage, or dead weight flagged it), the pair to merge with their similarity score, the digest or consolidated memory with its body rendered, the reproject's source and destination, the rekind's from and to kinds, the split's children and shared parent, and the knowledge gap card with the queries agents kept searching for in vain - applying that one opens a task; nothing is written until someone writes the memory.

Split batches are grouped by plan and reviewed together, setup card first, with Apply whole plan and Dismiss all N.

Under the head and its status line (below), one line says who may apply a proposal and which kinds apply automatically, with a link to Settings › Gardener, and Ask for a cleanup is a button that unfolds the ask box (with no chat model configured it is one line pointing at Settings); the queue follows, as a rail of proposals beside the reader. From the Standard level, Type (All, Split plans, Errors & gaps, Memory cleanup, Plan settlements, Digests: ?group=) and Source (All, Asked by you, Background: ?src=) narrow the rail. The reader says why each proposal was raised in a plain sentence. A merge shows both memories side by side - each body, when it last changed, when it was last delivered and how often - and Swap keeps the other one instead; an archive shows the memory's body, who wrote it, when it last changed and when it was last delivered. A memory the request may not read is not shown. A rail row says asked by you or background. Each rail section offers Dismiss all N and, when every proposal in it can be undone and none asks to be read first, Apply all N. Both ask in the page. Apply all takes exactly the rows shown, so a proposal raised after the page rendered is never applied unseen; Dismiss all takes the section as the Source filter narrows it. Each proposal lands in the decision history with its own Undo. A section holding a consolidation never offers Apply all. On the Gardener a applies the open proposal and x dismisses it.

The decision history opens with Applied automatically: every proposal automatic apply applied that is still applied, uncapped, each with its Undo (/console/gardener/decisions#gardener-auto). Every other decision is paged below it, so each appears once.

A status line under the head says what the background passes are doing: when the last pass ran and when the next one is due, each check a pass skips and why (dedup with no embeddings, digest with no chat model, a pass the config turns off), and any check that failed. An empty queue reads "The garden is tidy" only after a pass that ran every check; otherwise it says what did not run. Run a pass now starts the passes without waiting for the next one; it is refused while a pass runs. With gardener.enabled: false the line reads "Suggestions are off", no pass is offered, and the upkeep the same schedule carries (idle sessions reaped, old tool events pruned, retrieval stats refreshed) still runs. The line carries no counts: a pass spans every project, a locked one included.

The reader's actions are Apply change (which asks in the page first when it cannot be undone), Dismiss suggestion, Hide forever (from the Standard level), Retarget (reproject cards only, from the Standard level) and Swap (merge cards only); a split plan's are Apply whole plan and Dismiss all N. Dismissing answers the evidence in front of you - the pattern comes back if it recurs; hiding answers the pattern itself. A proposal changes nothing until it is applied - by you here, by an agent with gardener_apply while agents may apply proposals, or, for a kind you turned on under Apply by themselves, by automatic apply - and every decision records who made it. The newest ten land in Recently decided with an Undo; the decision history (/console/gardener/decisions) pages through all of them, newest first, with the outcome, who decided (you; an agent, by its session's name when a session made the call; automatic apply; the gardener settling a proposal whose memory had gone inactive; or unknown for a decision made before this was recorded), the note or task an apply produced, and Undo wherever it can be taken back. A hide is additionally listed under Hidden forever, where Unhide lifts the block without returning the proposal to the queue. The ask box under Ask for a cleanup only ever produces more proposals for this same queue. A request recognized as a project split is planned as a split directly - the plan batch appears below like any other. When the split's source project cannot be matched, an inline follow-up asks you to pick the project and plans the split from there; nothing is retyped.

Who may decide. Two switches on Settings, Gardener govern this queue. Agents may apply proposals is on by default (gardener.agents_may_apply). Turned off, gardener_apply refuses an agent's apply, dismiss and hide, gardener_proposals says the switch is off, and the decisions on this screen refuse an agent's process on the peer_auth socket and a paired device; your browser, your own terminal and the bearer key keep working. It stops an agent's ordinary calls and is not a wall: whoever holds the bearer key passes. Apply by themselves is off by default (gardener.auto_apply). It names the kinds - from memory_wanted, tool_error, abandon_plan and ship_plan, each reversible and only opening a task or retagging a plan note - that a pass applies by itself the moment it raises one. Such a decision is recorded as automatic apply, listed in the decision history with Undo, and counted on the Overview (N proposals applied automatically, since your last decision here). It waits for you instead while write screening's lockdown is on, when screening would hold the task text it lands, and for a proposal about a locked or fenced project. Only a pass's new proposals are applied by themselves: one already waiting, or one you undid, stays for you.

See The gardener for what each proposal type means.

Held

/console/held - while write screening is on, at every level (whoever turns it on must reach what it holds).

The owner's queue of agent writes kept out of the corpus. Each card says what the write would do (a constraint memory, a note, a delete, a gardener apply), which project, tool and session it came from (the project and the session link to their pages), and why it was held - each reason code with its meaning in words, the most serious first, each in its kind's color (a secret red, an injection marker orange, hidden text violet, hidden characters pink, an unlisted link indigo, an encoded blob teal, a binding-rule policy amber, a restricted account's proposal blue); the card's edge takes its most serious reason's color. Below that is the write exactly as an agent would read it: every hidden character spelled out as [U+XXXX], and secrets redacted, so the page can be reviewed and captured without the credential it holds. What each reason matched is marked in the text in that reason's color (hover a mark for its reason), and where matches overlap - an override phrase inside a hidden comment - the marks nest, so none hides another. The Review and Changed outside Seamless cards mark their findings the same way.

A held update of an existing memory or note opens on What releasing changes instead: a line diff of the write against the file as it stands now, each removed line marked - and each added line +, unchanged lines beyond three either side of a change folded into a count, with the same treatment and marks. The whole write follows, folded. A write that matches the current file line for line says so. A held new item shows its text alone.

  • Release lands it through the files layer as the agent wrote it, and the memory reads [owner-confirmed] in briefings from then on. A held supersede releases both halves together; a held delete removes the memory; a held gardener apply applies the proposal. When the target changed after the write was held, only Discard is offered: a release would silently undo that later change.
  • Discard lands nothing and erases the held text.

At the top, Lockdown says whether lockdown is on and what holds it, with the switch; a lockdown the configured lockdown file holds says so, and only that file going lifts it.

Below the queue, Changed outside Seamless lists the memory and note files the drift watch quarantined - changed or planted on disk by something other than Seamless - with their verdict codes, the sessions they were injected into before, and their text with the same treatment as a held write. Accept records one as it stands and lets agents receive it again. Review counts the review's verdicts (safe, flagged, not reviewed), lists each flagged item the same way with Mark safe, and offers Re-run review.

Sessions that read outside text lists every session an agent guard marked, with its reason and a Clear mark button - the only way a mark comes off. Recently decided keeps the last twenty releases and discards, without their text. The sidebar badge counts what is waiting.

Proposals from restricted accounts. Under peer_auth, a restricted local account's change to a constraint, convention, protocol or stage waits here too, as a proposal: its card says "Proposed by account ", and its button reads Promote instead of Release. Promoting lands it exactly as written, still labeled with the account; seam promote does the same from your terminal. While write screening is off, a daemon that lists restricted accounts still serves this screen, showing the proposals only - no lockdown, review or session marks - and the sidebar badge counts the proposals.

Elsewhere on the console, a memory, note, task, session or trial that a restricted account wrote carries a small "written by account " chip (a task whose title or body the account rewrote, "updated by account ", until you have rewritten all of its text; a status change or a claim moves neither chip), including search results, a lab's trial list and the project workspace's tabs; events and a session's activity timeline carry none. Your own items show none.

System

/console/system

Every part of Seamless on this server, drawn as one 3D base: the doors where agents and you come in (MCP, hooks, the peer_auth socket, the listener, the console, A2A), the work the daemon does (retrieval, tasks and plans, sessions, labs, approvals, write screening, updates, commit records, the metadata feed, URL capture, the gardener, lifecycle), the core that keeps knowledge on disk (the database, the file watcher, memory and note files, embeddings, the search index, the chat model, backups, the event log), and the outside services it calls (the LLM provider, GitHub releases).

  • State is the server's. Each part is running, quiet (on, with nothing in the event log for the last 15 minutes), needs attention, or off - drawn grey, with what turning it on takes. The header counts each state; click a count to light only those parts.
  • Motion is evidence. A part moves only while it works, and light runs along a trace only along the path a recorded event's data took: a memory write runs from MCP through the memory files, the watcher and the database to the search index, and on to embeddings and the provider. With nothing recorded the view is still and draws no frames.
  • Pick a part - on the deck or in the list under it - for its readout: what it does, its numbers for the last 24 hours, events per minute for the last 30, its settings, the parts it works with, and the screen that holds more. #<part> on the URL opens one directly.
  • Light on the GPU. It draws only while something changes, never while the tab is hidden or the view is scrolled away, keeps to a pixel budget on very large displays, and asks for the low-power GPU. Still (and the system's reduced-motion setting) keeps everything in place.
  • Without WebGL the deck is not drawn: the page says so in one line, the list of parts below is the page, and picking a part opens its readout above the list.

It is a Standard screen: Basic installs reach it by URL.

Privacy

/console/privacy

What your agents can reach on this server, what one could do if it were compromised, and where each project's knowledge may go.

  • Your setup - whether Seamless runs as your own account or as its own (peer_auth), and five protection layers: project fences, write screening, Seamless in its own account, locked projects, and a restricted agent account, each on, off, or waiting on an earlier one.
  • Who can reach what - the machine drawn as a plan: rooms are OS accounts, walls are what the operating system enforces, doors are how Seamless is reached. Switch between your account, a dedicated account and a dedicated account with restricted agents, and turn on Compromised agent to see how far one gets in each: in your own account it reads every project's files directly, sealed ones too, and takes the bearer key; in a dedicated account the data folder is out of its reach and a locked project waits for your approval.
  • Where knowledge is allowed to go - your projects around the global scope, with the flows each fence allows.
  • The four fences - open, confidential, sealed and locked, always all four, empty or not: what each promises, what kind of project belongs there, the projects in it, and how to put a project there. A locked project shows by name and counts only. Under peer_auth the Locked card also lists every confidential or sealed project not locked yet, each linked to its lock page (/console/lock/<project>); without it the card says what locking needs.
  • Find the fence for a project - three yes-or-no questions that end in a recommendation and its command.
  • What to do next - the steps that would tighten this server, in order.

It reads; it changes nothing. It is a Standard screen: Basic installs reach it by URL.

Devices

/console/devices

Only on a server that serves other computers (TLS, a bind beyond loopback, or a server_url naming another host); elsewhere the page and its routes do not exist. The computers paired with this server, and how to pair another (the guide):

  • Pair a computer - this server's address and its certificate's fingerprint, and Get a pairing code: a code shown once, valid for 10 minutes and for one computer, with the client one-liners, which carry the fingerprint for setup on the other computer to compare. The code works once, so the line left in that computer's shell history is dead after use. Without peer_auth the page says the code is the approval. Where this server's address is plain http to another host the page says pairing needs TLS, and offers no code. Where it names a user the page shows it without the user, says to take it out of server_url, and offers no code. Where it is this computer's loopback (no server_url on a wildcard bind) the page says the one-liners carry it, so another computer cannot use them, and that server_url is the fix; it still offers a code, for a client on this computer.
  • Waiting for your approval - under peer_auth only: each computer that used a code, its fingerprint and until when it waits, with Approve with a passkey and Deny. Approving needs a signed-in browser on the passkey origin and an enrolled passkey; the page says which is missing.
