A relay paired with its one-time code alone, while peer_auth was off, waits here too once peer_auth.relays maps it: it is refused until Approve with a passkey approves it in place, the same device and certificate, so it need not pair again, and Revoke ends it. The JSON lists it under in_place, not paired. A revoked or expired relay is not offered.
  • Paired - each relay and key device: its key's fingerprint or the start of its key, when it paired, whether your passkey or its one-time code approved it, when it was last seen, and Revoke. A relay shows the uid its pairing recorded as yours on its computer; without peer_auth one that recorded none (paired before, or by a relay of an earlier release) is warned about: re-pair it to bind the owner's uid. From 14 days before this server's certificate expires, and past it, the section names every relay paired here: a renewal means re-pairing each relay.
  • Revoked and expired - what ended, when, and from where.

It shows at every level, in the sidebar's Server group; g then c opens it.

Settings

/console/settings?s=<section>

Settings is one section at a time, each shaped by what you came to do rather than by subsystem. A sub-nav on the left (a row of chips on a phone) switches sections in place, without reloading the page. Each row names its section and its state in a word or two, so you can tell from any section whether backups run or an update waits: the level (Experience), how many features are on, the version (Your setup, amber while semantic recall's settings have a mistake), Up to date, v0.7.3 ready, Checks off, Paused or Failed (Updates), when the last backup ran, Off, None yet or Failing (Backups), what the gardener may change without you (Gardener), the briefing preset or Custom, how many projects (Workspaces), and Semantic or Keywords only (Knowledge engine). Green is fine, amber is worth a look, red needs you. A row's tooltip is what the section is for. /console/settings alone opens Experience; an unknown ?s= is a 400 that names the valid sections. Which sections a level offers is in the matrix above; a section above your level still opens from a link, under the same note a hidden screen gets. Old /console/settings#... bookmarks land on the matching section.

Each section opens with one line: its title, a hint with the longer why, one sentence, and - where its values can be set here - the source chip, which says where they come from: Config file (the config file and its environment variables, or the build's default), or Set here with Reset, which hands them back to the config file. The chip's hint says more. A value the config file makes final reads Config file decides, said once in its section, and the control it governs is disabled. Switches save at once, with Undo in the toast (the shared part): Features, Updates, Gardener and Knowledge engine's ranking rows. A form with a typed value (Briefing, and the Backups schedule and folder) keeps a save bar that appears at the bottom once it has unsaved changes, with Save and Discard (which puts the form back exactly as the page loaded it); without JavaScript the bar is simply always there. GET /console/settings?format=json returns the whole payload whatever ?s= says, plus consoleLevel, consoleLevelOverridden, consoleLevelSource, and sectionStatus: each section's state as {"word", "tone"} by section id (ok, accent, quiet, warn or danger), every section at every level.

Experience

/console/settings?s=experience

The three levels side by side - Basic, Standard, Advanced - as cards of one height, the one in force marked In use. Each has a one-line pitch and chips for what it shows (Basic) or adds (the others): its screens, then its Settings sections, each with a gear. The finer controls a level adds inside pages fold into a +N details chip, whose hint lists them. All of it is generated from the same registries the sidebar and the page gates read, so a card cannot promise something the level does not do. Choosing one is the card's Use button (Use Standard, say), and it applies at once: the sidebar and the page update in place, and if the new level hides the screen you were on you land on the Overview with a note. The source chip says Config file, or Set here once a level is stored, whether you chose it in this console or the upgrade set it (its hint says which); Reset hands the choice back to console.level. Below the cards, one card holds two rows: Theme, and Keyboard (? for every shortcut, ⌘K to search or jump, and Show shortcuts, which opens the shortcut sheet). The theme is System, Light, or Dark, kept per browser. System is what a browser starts on: it follows your computer's light or dark appearance, and follows it live when it changes. Light and Dark pin one theme. The sidebar's sun and moon switch the same setting: under System they pin the theme opposite the one on screen, and picking System here goes back to following the computer.

Features

/console/settings?s=features

Optional features are the parts of Seamless you can switch on and off, and they ship off: a fresh install exposes none of them until you turn one on. The section is one row per feature: its icon, its name, a one-line description, a chip for the data it keeps when it holds any ("8 trials kept", "1 write held"), and its switch. The name's hint holds the rest: what the feature is, a generated sentence naming exactly what turning it off takes away ("Turning this off hides the Labs & Trials screens, ..."), and, while it holds data, what is kept ("Data kept: 12 trials across 3 labs"). A switch saves as soon as you flip it, with no Save button: the toast names the change ("Momentum is off. Agents see it from their next session.") and offers Undo. Without JavaScript the section keeps a Save features button.

There are six today:

Research labs & trials owns the Labs and Trials screens, the trials search scope, and the lab_open, trial_record, and trial_query MCP tools. Screens and tools move together on purpose, so an agent never sees a tool for a screen you switched off.

Momentum is gentle progress cues woven into existing screens -- plan finish lines, capture streaks, knowledge payoffs, and project growth -- judged from real activity, never invented. It owns no screens or tools of its own; turning it on adds seven surfaces where you already look:

  • Plan finish-line cards on the Overview attention strip: any plan at least 80% done gets one positive card naming the exact remaining steps ("seambench -- one step from shipped"), linking to the plan, with a thin progress bar drawn to the plan's exact done/total percent. The agent briefing's plan line carries the same emphasis, so agents are nudged to close it too.
  • The capture calendar on Sessions: a year of daily activity, cell intensity from sessions per day, a distinct dot on days that captured knowledge (a session left findings, a memory, a note, or a trial), and two quiet numbers -- the current capture streak and the longest ever. The streak counts covered days, so it rewards capture, not raw usage; a streak of seven covered days or more earns a small flame beside the number, and the number itself stays verbatim. The grid is an instrument, not wallpaper: hovering a cell reads out its day, clicking one focuses the session map on exactly that day (a clearable chip names the focus; picking a time window widens back out), and the grid is keyboard-walkable -- arrows move a day or a week, Enter focuses, all without a page reload.
  • Knowledge payoff moments: the first time a memory is read by a session other than the one that wrote it, the moment lands in the activity ledger ("gotcha chroma-boot-race just paid off for the first time") -- once per memory, ever -- and the Overview rail gains a Memory of the month panel naming the last 30 days' top-utility memory with the counts behind the claim.
  • Maturity stages on the project board and detail header: each project earns a latched stage -- seedling, sprouting, established, deep-rooted -- from real thresholds over age, memories, event volume, and reach. Stages never regress, and the pill's tooltip states exactly what the next stage asks for.
  • The plan-shipped settle on Plans: the task transition that closes a plan's last step -- wherever it lands, an agent shipping over MCP included -- mints a once-ever plan.shipped moment. The plan's row settles with a single wash when it happens while you are watching, the ledger renders it under its own flag icon, and the Plans header counts the local month: "Plans shipped this month: N".
  • Milestone moments in the activity ledger: a short latched set of honest firsts and counts -- a project's 100th/500th/1000th memory, its 1000th answered recall, its first supersession, its first shipped plan, and its birthdays -- each minted once ever and rendered under an award glyph with the exact claim ("100 memories written in seamless"). Milestones accumulate in the ledger only; there is no trophy screen.
  • Witnessed unlocks on Settings: a ranking project's "since" note in Knowledge engine upgrades to the date it unlocked, so a latch that used to flip silently is witnessed.

Motion keeps one register: every animation plays once -- on a live arrival or on first render -- and nothing loops except the existing pulse idioms. A moment already on screen when the page loads renders plain; only a new arrival over the live feed animates. prefers-reduced-motion stills all of it, and the shipped-plan settle is the ceiling: no confetti and no toasts, which belong to gamification's arcade on Now.

Momentum keeps the console's judged-numbers ethos: every number is real and verifiable, empty states say so honestly, and there are no punishment mechanics -- an inactive day is an empty cell, never a warning, and nothing nags or expires. Off (the default), none of it renders and none of it is computed: no latch moves and no moment is minted. Moments minted while it was on stay in the event history (nothing is ever deleted), though milestone rows leave the activity feeds until it returns.

Gamification is the arcade layer of the Now screen. Where momentum asks "is this knowledge practice building on itself?", gamification plays back "how hard is the fleet running right now?" - and an owner who enjoys one framing may find the other noisy, so they toggle separately. It owns no screens or tools of its own; turning it on adds four surfaces to Now:

  • The day tape: today's judged output - tasks closed, memories and notes written, plans touched, sessions started - each cell against its trailing 7-day daily average.
  • The personal-records rail: latched bests (most tasks closed in a day, most memories written in a day, most agents live at once). Records only ever move forward, like maturity stages; an unset record reads "today could be the day".
  • The hot-streak pulse: the last ten minutes' event count beside the titlebar pulse, catching fire past a fixed floor. The count is shown verbatim either way, so the claim stays verifiable.
  • Celebration moments: a record falling or a plan shipping its last step today renders a moment chip - and when one lands while you are watching, a toast and a brief confetti burst (skipped under reduced motion). A record crossing is minted into the event ledger at most once per record per day.

The same guardrails as momentum apply: every number is judged from recorded activity, never invented, and there are no punishment mechanics - a quiet day is an empty tape, never a warning. Off (the default), none of it is computed, no record latch is written, and the Now page carries zero trace of it.

Write screening is the only feature that changes what agents receive rather than what the console shows. On, every agent write to a memory or note is screened, the suspicious ones - and any change to a binding rule by a session that read outside text, and any supersede or delete of a constraint - wait on the Held screen instead of landing, and briefing and recall lines carry owner-confirmed or agent-written marks. Its row's chip counts the writes waiting; turning it off stops screening new writes and releases none of them. With restricted local accounts configured, the row's hint says the Held screen stays for their proposals and only its screening parts go. The write screening guide has the screens, the reasons and the events.

Repo locks owns the Locks screen, the locks_list, locks_declare, locks_acquire and locks_release MCP tools, and seam lock: locks on a repository's refs that agents declare once and hold while they land changes. Turning it off deletes no lock and no declaration.

Diary owns the Diary screen - a page for each day of work, at every level, the first row of the Work group - and one in-page surface, the Open in Diary link on a Sessions day view. Turn it on here, or with features.diary: true in the config file or SEAMLESS_FEATURES_DIARY=true. Off (the default), there is no sidebar row, palette entry, shortcut, link or script, and /console/diary answers with the switched-off page. It owns no MCP tools. The token record underneath is kept either way: the usage ledger and the event log the Diary reads are written whether it is on or off, so the history is there the moment you turn it on. Turning it on adds one cost that is not presentation: while it is on, a Claude Code prompt keeps its session's usage ledger current, read after the prompt is answered, at most once every three minutes a conversation (mid-session usage). With it off, every hook answers and writes exactly as before.

Nothing is ever deleted. Switching a feature off gates exposure and nothing else: the trials stay in the database, its screens answer with a short "switched off" page that links back here (a JSON caller gets a 403), and switching it back on restores every surface exactly as it was. That is what the data-kept chip on each row is for - it reports the feature's own rows whether it is on or off.

When the change lands depends on the surface:

Surface When
The console Immediately - nav entries, screens, the search scope, and the overview tiles appear or disappear on the next render.
A tool call Immediately - a disabled feature's tool is refused as an unknown tool, whatever list the caller is holding.
A hook Immediately - the Diary's mid-session usage read follows the switch from the next Claude Code prompt, with no restart.
The agent briefing The next session start - momentum's finish-line emphasis reads the same stored override the console gates on.
A client's tool list The next time it lists tools, in practice its next session. Seamless declares listChanged: false and sends no tool-list notification, so a connected client keeps the list it already has.
The client-side skill The next seamlessd install-hooks run. The daemon does not reach into ~/.claude/skills on a toggle, so seamlessd doctor raises an info line while a skill for a disabled feature is still sitting in a client's skill home.

Each save writes a stored override row in the database - the same layer the briefing form uses. It wins over file and env, never touches your config file, and holds until Reset on the source chip clears it; reset means back to the file/env configuration, which unless you set features: there is off.

One override can be in force without you having set it. Upgrading an installation that already holds trial data seeds the override with research on, so a feature that now ships off does not disappear from under data you were already using. That is why the chip's hint says the choice is stored here, by a save or by that upgrade, rather than crediting you with it - and reset clears it like any other. At Basic the section keeps the rows, what each hides, and the data-kept chip, and leaves out the agent tool names and the source chip.

Your setup

/console/settings?s=setup

What runs where, as one card of rows. Each value is a chip or a short path, the detail is one hover away in a hint, and each row whose value can change links to the section that changes it:

  • Version, with the Updates section's state chip (Up to date, v0.7.3 ready, Checks off and so on) and a link to Updates;
  • Running on: the machine, and under peer_auth the account the daemon runs as;
  • Config file, with a copy button and Open in editor - or None, when the daemon runs on its defaults and environment variables;
  • Data folder, with a copy button, and the database's size (its path in the hover);
  • Agents connected: one chip per agent client that has recorded sessions, with when it was last active;
  • Semantic recall: semantic and the model, or keywords only, with what to do about it in a hint and a link to the troubleshooting guide; the row links to Knowledge engine;
  • Backups, where a backup service runs: the Backups section's state chip, how often they run and how many are kept, and a link to Backups;
  • Gardener: agents apply or only you apply, how many kinds apply by themselves, and suggestions off while its passes are off - its cadence in a hint - with a link to the Gardener section.

A path under your home folder reads ~, and a long one is shortened in the middle; its hover and its copy button hold the whole path. Links to these docs close the section. No budgets or policy numbers: those live in Knowledge engine.

Updates

/console/settings?s=updates

The automatic update check and automatic updates, what is true first.

While something needs you, one alert card opens the section, worst first, each item with its action and its details in a hint: the update checker stopped after an internal error (restart the daemon); and on an install that updates itself, automatic updates paused themselves and releases held back after you went back to an older one (one Resume lifts both), releases automatic updates skip, and the backoff after a failed attempt, with when they try again. Last comes the last attempt, while it failed, rolled back or was interrupted below the release it tried, could not be rolled back cleanly, or applied with warnings (with seamlessd install-hooks, which re-wires your agents, and a copy button). Its line says what it meant - and, when the updater refused to start, the fix - and a skip or a backoff for the same release joins that line. Its log path has a copy button, and its hint holds the updater's own error: the one place in the console either appears.

The first card shows the installed version, the kind of build and who installed it; the newest release, with its date and release notes, or Up to date; and an attempt that needs nothing from you, in one quiet line. On an install that updates itself, Update to v0.7.3 now installs the newest release at once after a confirm - skipping the soak, the idle wait, skipped releases and the backoff - and the daemon restarts to finish. While an update runs, the card says Updating to v0.7.3 and its stage, and Confirming v0.7.3 once the new version serves. On an install that does not update itself, the card ends with To update: the command that does, with a copy button, and why this install is only told in a hint.

Then the switches, which save as you flip them, with Undo in the toast:

  • Check for new releases. Its hint says what a check sends: one anonymous request to api.github.com every few hours, and nothing at all while it is off. Its line says when the daemon last checked and checks next, or a streak of failed checks and why, the error in a hint. Check now asks GitHub once, right away (not more than once a minute).
  • Install updates by themselves, on an install that updates itself: the installer's, or a peer_auth system daemon in the guide's layout. Its line names the next update and what it waits for - the soak, live agent sessions, or a lull after its deadline - and its hint says how an update installs and the command that updates by hand.
  • Owner-signed releases, with update.release_signers set in the config file or environment: a required chip, the file in its hint, and the last release it refused and why: it carried no owner's signature, was signed by a key the file does not list, or its signature did not verify. Without the key the row is not there. The console can neither set nor clear it.

The source chip says who decided the switches: Config file (the config file, or the build's default), or Set here with Reset when this console set either switch; its hint says which. Turning a switch off from here always works for you; an agent's process on the peer_auth socket, and a paired device but for your own hands through a relay, may turn checks and automatic updates on, never off. update.check: false in the config file or SEAMLESS_UPDATE_CHECK is final and decides the whole section: the head's chip reads Config file decides, the switches are locked, and saving checks on is refused - false promises no update traffic at all. update.auto: false is final for its own switch, so its Config file decides chip sits beside it.

When a newer release is out, the Overview health strip's version fact turns into v0.7.2 -- v0.7.3 available and links here - its hover says whether it installs by itself, and when - and a toast announces it if the console is open when the daemon finds it. While an update runs, the fact reads v0.7.2 -- updating to v0.7.3, and once v0.7.3 is serving and the updater is only confirming it, v0.7.3 -- confirming the update (the first card says Confirming v0.7.3 too). The daemon re-reads the updater's record every few seconds while an update runs, so both clear soon after it is confirmed. For a day after the daemon starts on a new version, every page carries a banner - "Seamless updated to v0.7.3 (from v0.7.2)" - with the release notes and Got it, which hides it in this browser. It also says when Codex's hooks changed with the update (re-approve them in Codex's /hooks) or the installer reported warnings (run seamlessd install-hooks). For a week after automatic updates pause themselves, or after an update the daemon started does not apply, every page also carries a warning banner pointing here. While automatic backups are in trouble too, the two warnings share one row with one Got it.

Backups

/console/settings?s=backups

Scheduled backups of the whole instance into one folder you choose, the backups found there, and restore. Backups in the console walks through it; this is what each card holds, what is true first.

While something needs you, one alert card opens the section, worst first: the backup service stopped after an internal error; Automatic backups are failing - how many automatic runs failed in a row and since when, the last one's error, and its reason in a hint - with Try again, which runs the schedule's backup now; and Your backup did not finish, with its error.

The first card says when the last backup ran - Backed up 2h ago, with its size and what it holds in a hint - or No backup yet, or the backup under way. Its line says when the next one runs (or Nothing changed since, with when it checks next) or that automatic backups are off, how many are kept, and the newest backup's size. The folder is a short chip with a copy button, the whole path in its hover, and Back up now makes a backup marked Made by you whatever the schedule says. Its mark is green while backups run on time, amber while automatic backups have made none yet, are overdue or are failing, red when the service stopped, and grey while they are off.

The schedule, a form with a Save bar, since it holds typed values:

  • Back up automatically, a switch. A run is skipped when nothing has changed since the last backup, or when the disk is short of room.
  • How often: Hourly, 6 hours, Daily or Weekly. An interval set in the config file (anything from 1h to 720h) shows among them as itself.
  • Keep, 1 to 100 automatic backups. Its hint says older automatic backups are deleted after the next one, and backups you make yourself and safety backups never are.
  • Folder, with a live check as you type (it only looks, never writes) and chips for the places on this machine this account can write to: iCloud Drive, cloud folders and external disks on macOS, Dropbox and external disks on Linux, OneDrive and other drives on Windows, and Seamless's data folder.

Save stores only what differs from the settings in force; a new folder is created and tested with a write first. The source chip in the section's head says where the values come from: Config file (the config file, or the build's default), or Set here, whose hint names the fields you set and whose Reset makes the settings follow the config file again.

Available backups, the list, newest first: the backups in the chosen folder and in Seamless's data folder (~/.seamless/backups, where the safety and pre-update backups stay). Each row has:

  • when, the kind in words - Automatic, Made by you, Before restore, Before updating from v0.8.1 or Exported - the size, and the machine it came from when another Seamless made it;
  • What it holds: the file's path, and per project the memories, notes, tasks and sessions, beside vs now, how many more or fewer memories and notes the project holds now. A locked project shows its name and the backup's counts, never what it holds now. A project that is no longer here says so, and one that is only here now shows dashes;
  • Restore… and Delete, which asks in place first. An iCloud placeholder (download it in Finder first) and a backup a newer Seamless made (update to restore it) cannot be restored and say why.

The list's title carries a hint: where these backups come from, and that a locked project shows what the backup holds of it, never what it holds now.

Restore… opens a confirm card in the backup's row, with a link that works without script:

  • it compares the backup with now (how many more or fewer memories, notes and sessions this install holds);
  • two choices: Replace all data with this backup (your current data is saved as a backup first, so you can undo it) or Only bring back what's missing (nothing you have now changes). A knowledge-only backup offers only the merge;
  • what a restore leaves alone: locks, passkeys, repo routes and console settings stay as they are now, and no project's privacy is loosened;
  • Restore, or Restore with passkey under the peer_auth gate. Without a usable passkey, the card names why and shows the terminal command instead, with a copy button.

Then a progress card lists the steps, numbered, each done, under way or still to come: Checking the backup, Preparing the restored data (replace) or Saving your current data (merge), Restarting Seamless, Done, and for a replace, Saving your previous data as a backup. The page waits through the restart and draws the section again in place. Cancel restore is offered while a restore is staged. On Windows, the card names seamlessd restart, to run within an hour, after which a staged restore is dropped.

After the restart, the result card says what was restored, where the previous data was saved, and anything the restore kept of today (a stricter privacy setting, locked projects the backup did not have), with Undo this restore - the confirm card for the safety backup - and Dismiss. A restore that did not finish, expired or stopped partway says so there instead.

Elsewhere:

  • Settings > Your setup has a Backups row: the Backups section's state chip, how often they run, and how many are kept.
  • Every page carries an alert while automatic backups are in trouble, linking here. Automatic backups are failing. appears when two automatic runs in a row did not finish, with the first failure's time and the reason. Automatic backups are overdue. appears when none has finished for three intervals. Got it hides it in this browser until a new episode begins.
  • System draws backups as a core part, on, off, failing or overdue.

Gardener

/console/settings?s=gardener

Who may act on the gardener's proposals, and which apply by themselves: a Basic section, beside the Gardener screen, whose sentence about who may decide links here. Its source chip says Config file (the file, the environment, or the default) or Set here, whose Reset hands both switches back to the config file; the chip's hint says where each one comes from. Both switches save the moment you flip them, with Undo in the toast (without JavaScript, each card keeps a Save button), and apply at once, with no restart.

  • Agents may apply proposals, on by default (gardener.agents_may_apply). Off, only you decide: gardener_apply refuses an agent's apply, dismiss and hide, and so do the Gardener screen's decisions from an agent's process or a paired device. agents_may_apply: false in the config file or environment is final: the switch is disabled, with a Config file decides chip beside it.
  • Apply by themselves: one switch per kind a pass may apply the moment it raises one - a task for a knowledge gap or for a recurring error, a finished plan marked shipped, a stale captured plan abandoned - each with how Undo takes it back, and a count of how many are on. Every other kind always waits for you. The group's hint says when a kind you turned on waits for you anyway: while lockdown is on, when write screening would hold it, and for a locked or fenced project.
  • Runs every N min: the gardener's cadence, with suggestions on or suggestions off (gardener.enabled) and upkeep always: idle sessions are reaped, old tool events pruned and retrieval stats refreshed on the same clock either way. Tuning, from the config file folds the six values the passes use: the dedup threshold, when a memory and when a captured plan count as stale, the digest window, how long tool events are kept, and when a session counts as idle. They change in the config file or environment, then a restart.

The section's sub-nav state says what the gardener may change without you: Proposes only, Only you decide (agents may not apply), 2 of 4 automatic, Suggestions off, or Unreadable (amber) while the stored switches cannot be read. An old link to the switches' place in Knowledge engine (?s=engine#settings-gardener) opens this section. Your setup shows both as chips, with a link to this section.

Briefing

/console/settings?s=briefing

What every new agent session starts with. Where the section is wide enough (a desktop window), the form is on the left and the preview beside it, in view while you scroll the knobs; narrower, the preview follows the form.

Three presets lead the form under Start from - Lean (the binding rules and the freshest memories), Balanced (exactly the defaults), and Rich (more rules in full, more recent work, and the family) - each card showing the numbers that set it apart until the preview prices it for its project ("~780 tokens"). in use marks the preset your saved values equal. Picking one fills the form; nothing is saved until you save. Below them, Fine-tune holds every knob in compact groups - Memories, Recent work, Plans and stages, Project family, Ranking, and Ceiling. Each knob is a label, an (i) hint that says what it does, and its value with its unit; at 0 the unit says what 0 means instead ("any age", "off", "budget", "always", "all in full"), and follows as you type. The form marks the preset its values equal, or Custom when they match none, and re-marks it as you edit.

Saving writes a runtime override row in the DB. It layers over the file/env values and wins until reset, and it applies from the next session start - no daemon restart. It never touches your config file, so seamless.yaml stays the thing you wrote. The token budget (budgets.max_briefing_tokens) is not a briefing knob and no preset moves it. The form validates: a non-numeric knob or a value that fails Briefing.Validate() comes back as an error flash, not a silently-dropped save.

The preview shows the <seam-briefing> a new session in one project would start with, under the values the form holds right now, saved or not (unsaved values says when they differ from what is saved). Pick a preset or change a knob and it follows within a moment. It also shows the token estimate against budgets.max_briefing_tokens and the hard cap, and flags a briefing that runs over the budget (only constraints, pinned stages, and starred rows can put it there) or would be cut at the cap. The project picker lists the registered projects and opens on the one your agents worked in last. When the page opens and when you pick another project, the preview also prices each preset for that project: presets=1 on the request adds one assembly per preset and a presets list (key, tokens) to the JSON answer. A preview is a read: it saves nothing, records no event, and no agent receives it, so it never counts toward retrieval stats or utility. Values the save would refuse, it refuses with the same message. For scripts, GET /console/settings/briefing/preview?project=<slug>&format=json previews the saved values. POST to the same path, with the form's fields plus project, previews unsaved ones. It is the one POST in the console that writes nothing, which is why it is not in the table of write routes above.

The Ranking group holds Use weight (utility_weight: utility's share of the briefing sort key; 0 restores pure recency) and Turns on (utility_mode: Per project arms each project as its demand history matures, Everywhere is every project now, Never is none). Where each project stands against the readiness gates is in Knowledge engine. See Sessions & briefings for how the blended order behaves once active.

Workspaces

/console/settings?s=workspaces

Which project each repository resolves to, and which projects share context. Project families are editable here: create, rename, edit, or delete the named groupings that seamlessd family manages from the CLI - the same project_families setting, so a change on either surface shows up on the other. Members are chosen from a closed picker of registered projects; the CLI is the route for pre-registering a slug that does not exist yet. Below it, one bounded directory lists every project with its repo routes, plus a Family column when any project has a family or a parent. A repo route ties a repository folder to a project: an agent that starts in that folder, or anywhere under it, works in that project. Find a project narrows the rows as you type, matching a slug, a name, or a route's path, and With repo routes keeps only the projects that have one. The switch is offered when some projects have a route and some do not, and starts on when more than 12 have none. Both narrow the rows in the page, with no reload; without JavaScript every row shows. At Advanced each route also names the machine it lives on, and repo paths that resolve to no project are listed under Repo routes with no project.

Knowledge engine

/console/settings?s=engine

How recall finds knowledge and how briefings rank it, in three cards. The gardener's switches and cadence have a section of their own, Gardener.

Recall - two rows. Semantic recall carries a state chip (semantic, keywords only, or misconfigured), the reason in its sub line, and the fix in its hint: switched off from this console; no embedding provider set up (the hint is Your setup's sentence: add a key, then restart; the daemon's own error stays in its log); or a config mistake, with the provider's error. The off/auto switch is a settings row read once at serve start, so the row flags a pending restart whenever the stored switch disagrees with the running process, and Switch off is offered only while there is something to switch off: embeddings running, or a cleared switch still waiting for that restart. The second row is the stored vectors, named by the model: their counts in one line (vectors, items not yet embedded, vectors on an old model), and By model, folded, while there is more than one model or a stale one. Re-embed all rewrites the corpus with the active model in the background, after a confirm in the page, and the row follows the pass in place while the page is open.

Ranking by use - chips count the projects that rank by use now, any that rank from the gardener's next pass, the forced ones, and the ones still building. Only the projects that rank, are ready to, or are forced get a row: its uses, memories used and days of history, a small meter of those three gates against their thresholds (green once met), and Auto / On / Off, which saves at once, with Undo, and returns to the row. A forced project stays listed until it is set back to Auto. The rest fold under one row ("42 projects still building their history"), each with what it still needs ("needs 7 more events, 3d more history") and the same segment. The hint gives the thresholds. When Turns on in Briefing is Everywhere or Never, the card says it decides for every project, and these choices wait until it is back to Per project.

Storage - read-only, with a lock by its name: chips for the data folder (with Copy), the database (size on disk including the WAL, and schema version), and the briefing and recall budgets. Its hint says they are set in the config file or environment and read at start, and gives the database's path and the tool-event cap.

See Configuration for what each knob does, and Sessions & briefings for what they tune.

Event detail

/console/events/{id}

What a Recent-activity or timeline row links to: a compact event review workspace with the event's agent/session attribution, verbatim injected or transport content, surfaced memories resolved to their live index entries (or flagged missing), remaining payload fields, and raw JSON (the last two at the Advanced level; ?format=json always carries them). The Interactions inspector uses the same content model in a side pane; opening the full page adds context without changing the underlying event.

What it is about. The item an event names is resolved by the event's kind and linked: the memory it wrote or read, the note, the task (with its state), the trial, the session, the plan, or the gardener proposal. A gardener event also names what its proposal is about - the memory it would archive, the two it would merge, the plan it would settle - and its title says so: "proposed archiving a memory:" and the memory's name. A pending proposal links to it on the Gardener screen, a decided one to the decision history. Everything resolves through what this console reads: an item it cannot read - deleted, or in a locked project - is shown by its kind and id alone, never named. Times read in this browser's own clock, and the page's title is the event's headline.

Errors

A bad or stale URL renders a styled, layout-wrapped error page with a way back, rather than dropping you on a bare 404 page not found -- including any /console/ path no route claims, which gets a search box and links to the common destinations. A 404 names the missing entity and a 400 names the bad parameter and its valid values. A 500 stays generic in the browser - the detail is in the log, not the response. Fragment fetches (?peek=1) get a fragment-shaped error, since a full page injected into the reading panel would nest the whole console inside itself.
